section: SLR 01 – Structure and function of the processor
title: Flipped – Core components of the CPU
hints: Candidates need to have an understanding of the purpose and function of the core components of a processor.
Candidates need to understand the role and components of the ALU.
Candidates need to understand the purpose and function or registers within the processor, including the PC, accumulator, MAR, MDR and CIR.
Candidates need to understand the purpose, function and role of the data, address and control buses in the processor.
Candidates need to understand how assembly language makes use of registers, and how data and addressed are transferred between registers.

definitions.definition: The processor that **fetches, decodes and executes** instructions, controlling and processing the computer's operations.
The CPU component that performs **arithmetic calculations** and logical comparisons/operations.
The CPU component that decodes instructions and coordinates their execution by **sending control signals**.
A small, very fast memory location **inside the CPU**, used to hold data, addresses or instructions currently in use. Faster than accessing RAM.
A set of connections that **carries** data, addresses or control signals between computer components.

points: The ALU carries out arithmetic (such as addition) and logic (such as AND or comparison) operations; it can update status flags.
The CU decodes the current instruction and issues signals to coordinate the ALU, registers, memory and input/output devices.
The PC holds the address of the next instruction; it is **incremented by one** during the fetch stage. Can be changed by a jump or branch instruction.
The accumulator temporarily stores **results of ALU operations**. The MAR holds a memory address to be read from or written to; the MDR holds data being transferred to or from memory.
The CIR holds the instruction currently being decoded/executed, after it has been fetched from memory.

The address bus carries addresses from the MAR to the RAM; the data bus carries data and instructions between the processor and memory; the control bus carries signals such as memory read and memory write.

In assembly language, operands can identify registers or memory locations; instructions transfer values between registers and memory, and the processor uses buses to carry the corresponding data and addresses.

section: SLR 01 – Structure and function of the processor
title: Flipped – Fetch Decode Execute Cycle
hints: Candidates need to understand the purpose and stages within the FDE cycle.
Candidates need to understand how and when the registers are used within this cycle, and how and where data and addresses are transmitted to/from in each part of this cycle.

definitions.definition: The repeated sequence by which a processor fetches an instruction, interprets it and carries it out.
A register containing the **address of the next instruction** to be fetched. Incremented by one during the fetch stage. Can be changed by a jump or branch instruction.
A register holding the instruction currently being decoded and executed.
A register holding the address of the memory location currently being accessed.
A register holding data or an instruction being transferred to or from memory.
A register that temporarily holds results of ALU calculations, inputs + outputs and data come from RAM.

points: At the start of fetch, the address in the PC is copied to the MAR
The address in the MAR is sent on the address bus and a memory read signal is sent from the CU to RAM via the control bus.
The instruction at that address is transferred from memory over the data bus to the MDR, then copied to the CIR.
The PC is incremented so that it points to the next sequential instruction; a branch or jump may later replace its value.
During decode, the CU interprets the opcode in the CIR and determines the operation, operands and required control signals.
During execute, the CU coordinates the required data transfers and operation; the ALU may process operands and place a result in a register or memory.
If an operand is in memory, its address is placed in the MAR and the data is transferred via the MDR; the address and data buses carry these separately.
The cycle repeats for each instruction, with interrupts potentially being checked/serviced at defined points.
e.g. SUB one, the address of one is placed in the MAR, the value at that address is fetched into the MDR, then subtracted from the accumulator and the result stored back in the accumulator.
STA stores the value in the accumulator to a given memory address
LDA loads a value from a specified location into the accumulator
BRP loop - if the value in the accumulator is positive, the PC is set to the address of loop, otherwise execution continues with the next instruction.
one DAT 1 - stores the value 1 in memory at the address labelled one, which can be used as an operand in other instructions.

section: SLR 01 – Structure and function of the processor
title: Flipped – Factors affecting CPU performance
hints: The factors affecting the performance of the CPU: clock speed, number of cores, cache.
Candidates need to understand how the performance of the CPU can be affected by many factors.
Candidates need to understand how and why the performance is affected by the clock speed, the number of cores and the size and speed of the cache.

definitions.definition: The number of processor clock cycles per second, measured in hertz (commonly GHz).
An independent processing unit within a CPU that can fetch, decode and execute instructions.
Small, fast memory in or close to the CPU that stores copies of frequently or recently used instructions and data.

points: Performance of a CPU means how quickly it can complete a given workload, which depends on the number of instructions executed per second.
A higher clock speed can allow more cycles per second, so more instructions can be executed per second so programs take less time to complete, provided the processor can use those cycles effectively.
More cores can execute separate tasks or threads in parallel (at the same time), improving throughput when software and workload can be divided between them.
Extra cores may give little benefit to a program that cannot be parallelised; coordination overhead can also reduce gains.
Cache is faster to access than RAM. This reduces the bottleneck. A cache hit supplies data quickly and reduces waiting for main memory.
A larger cache can increase the chance that required data is cached, while a faster cache reduces access time; cache size and speed are constrained by cost and processor design.
Increasing clock speed, number of cores and cache size can help. Other methods include more RAM, using GPUs and distributed systems.

section: SLR 01 – Structure and function of the processor
title: Flipped - Pipelining
hints: The use of pipelining in a processor to improve efficiency.

definitions.definition: A processor technique that overlaps stages of several instructions so different instructions are processed simultaneously at different stages.
The process of clearing the pipeline of instructions that are no longer needed, typically due to a branch or other control flow change.

points: A typical pipeline divides instruction processing into stages such as fetch, decode and execute.
While one instruction is executing, a later instruction can be decoded and another fetched, increasing instruction throughput and means more of the processor's resources are utilized simultaneously.
Pipelining improves the number of instructions completed over time; it does not reduce the time taken by one individual instruction.
Reduces the amount of time the CPU has to wait and reduces idle time
Flushing the pipe can be needed with branches. This reduces the performance benefit.
This is **not** the same as parallel processing: pipelining overlaps stages of different instructions, while parallel processing uses multiple cores to execute multiple instructions at the same time.

section: SLR 01 – Structure and function of the processor
title: Flipped – Von Neumann & Harvard architecture
hints: Von Neumann, Harvard and contemporary processor architecture.

Candidates need to have an understanding of the Von Neumann and Harvard architectures. They should be aware of the different approaches the architectures take to storing instructions and data in memory and the benefits of each approach.

Candidates will not be asked about specific aspects of “contemporary processor architecture” unless explicitly named in the specification. They may, however, be asked to show an awareness of how contemporary processors differ from a pure Von Neumann architecture in more open questions.

definitions.definition: An architecture in which instructions and data share the same memory and buses. Features a single CU and single ALU
An architecture with separate memories and buses for instructions and data.
The limit on throughput caused by instructions and data sharing a path between the processor and memory.

points: In a Von Neumann system, the same memory stores program instructions and data, which are transferred over shared buses.
A shared memory/bus design is comparatively simple and flexible, but the processor cannot generally fetch an instruction and access data simultaneously over the same path.
Harvard architecture separates instruction and data memories/buses, allowing instruction fetch and data access to occur at the same time.
Separate Harvard memories can have different widths or technologies optimised for instructions and data, but the design is more complex and less flexible in allocating memory.
Contemporary general-purpose processors are not always pure Von Neumann designs: they may use separate instruction and data caches or pipelines while retaining a shared main memory/address space.
A modified Harvard arrangement can combine Harvard-style internal caches/buses with Von Neumann-style main memory.
Contemporary CPUs can have e.g. multiple cores and onboard graphics to improve performance and throughput beyond the original Von Neumann design.

title: Flipped - CISC vs RISC
hints: Candidates need to understand the differences between the CISC and RISC processors and the key features and benefits of each.
They should be aware of the relative benefits of each architecture.

definitions.definition: Complex instruction set computer: a processor design with a relatively large set of instructions, including complex instructions.
Reduced instruction set computer: a processor design using a smaller, simpler set of instructions, often designed for fast execution.
The set of machine instructions that a processor can execute.

points: RISC instructions are generally simple so each instruction takes a single cycle to execute, aiding pipelining.
CISC instructions can take differing numbers of cycles and may be more complex to decode or pipeline; complex instructions can require more hardware.
CISC instructions can perform complex operations and may reduce the number of instructions needed for a program.
RISC programs may need more instructions for the same task, potentially increasing code size and memory traffic.
RISC processors have simpler hardware and can be cheaper and more power-efficient, which is useful in mobile or embedded systems.
CISC processors have more complex hardware that make them more expensive to design and manufacture. They can be more power-hungry, which is less suitable for mobile or embedded systems.
CISC can make assembly/program code compact; RISC can simplify processor implementation and support efficient high-throughput execution.

title: Flipped - GPUs and their uses
hints: Candidates need to understand the purpose of GPUs and what applications they are used for (candidates need to understand how GPUs are used to aid graphics, but also other applications for example their use in modeling, data mining, etc.).
Candidates should understand the benefits and using GPUs and why they are suited to certain tasks (specialist instructions, multiple cores and SIMD processing).

definitions.definition: A specialised processor designed to carry out many graphics or other suitable calculations in parallel.
Single instruction, multiple data: one instruction is applied simultaneously to multiple data items.
Executing multiple calculations or instruction streams at the same time using multiple processing resources.

points: GPUs accelerate graphics tasks such as transforming vertices, shading pixels and rendering images for display.
A GPU contains many processing cores, suited to applying similar operations to large numbers of data items at once.
SIMD allows one operation to be applied across a large data set, such as adjusting the colour of many pixels.
GPUs can accelerate non-graphics workloads with abundant independent calculations, including scientific modelling, simulation and data mining.
Specialist graphics instructions and high parallel throughput make GPUs effective for these workloads.
A GPU is less suited to tasks with sequential dependencies, frequent branching or little parallelism; transferring data between CPU and GPU can add overhead.
The CPU remains better suited to general-purpose, sequential control tasks, while a GPU acts as a specialised accelerator.
Using a GPU can increase performance of games making them more realistic and responsive, and can accelerate scientific simulations, machine learning and data analysis.
GPUs have dedicated memory and high bandwidth to support large data sets, but may require careful programming to achieve optimal performance.

title: Flipped - Multi-core & parallel systems
hints: Candidates need to understand what is meant by a parallel system and the benefits and limitations of parallel processing.
Candidates need to understand that parallel processing can be achieved through different methods (i.e. multiple processors in the same computer or distributed across multiple cores in a CPU or GPU).
Candidates need to understand the benefits of a multicore system in terms of parallel processing and running multiple programs at the same time.

definitions.definition: A computer system that uses multiple processing resources to execute parts of a workload simultaneously.
A single CPU chip containing two or more independent processing units. The units can independently process instructions at the same time.
A system in which processing is shared across multiple networked computers.
The amount of work completed in a given time period.
Processes happen at the same time. Uses time slicing to give the appearance of simultaneous execution on a single core.

points: Parallel processing may use multiple cores in one CPU, multiple processors in one computer, GPUs, or computers distributed across a network.
A multicore CPU can execute separate threads/programs at the same time, improving throughput and responsiveness when work can run concurrently.
A task must be divided into independent parts to benefit substantially; sequential work limits the speed-up.
Parallel tasks may need communication and synchronisation, adding overhead and creating contention for shared memory/resources.
Distributed systems can combine resources across machines and scale beyond one computer, but rely on network communication and are affected by latency or failure.
Running several programs concurrently improves overall use of the CPU, although it does not guarantee that each individual program finishes faster.
Parallel systems are useful for workloads such as simulations or image processing that can be split into many independent calculations.

title: Flipped - Input, output and storage devices
hints: Candidates need to have an understanding of a range of input, output and storage devices.
Candidates do not need to understand how the input and output devices work, but must be able to recommend appropriate devices for specific situations and be able to justify choices made.

definitions.definition: Hardware used to enter data or control signals into a computer system.
Hardware that presents information from a computer system to a user or another system.
Hardware that stores data and programs for later retrieval, either temporarily or persistently.

points: A keyboard is suitable for entering text; a mouse or touch screen is suited to selecting and manipulating on-screen items.
A microphone captures sound and a camera captures images/video; select them when the relevant analogue or visual data must be entered.
Sensors provide measurements such as temperature or pressure, useful for automated monitoring and control without manual entry.
A monitor displays visual output for interactive use; a printer produces hard copy, useful when a physical record is needed.
Speakers/headphones provide audio output; actuators can produce physical actions in a control system.
A magnetic hard disk or solid-state drive is appropriate for persistent, high-capacity storage; removable flash media is useful for portability and transfer.
Justify a device choice by matching required data, accuracy, speed, capacity, portability, durability, cost and environment to the scenario.

title: Flipped - Magnetic, flash and optical storage
hints: Candidates need to understand that there are different types of storage device.

They need to know about the characteristics of each type (magnetic, optical and flash) and understand the benefits and drawbacks of each, and be able to recommend an appropriate type of device for a given situation and justify the choice.

definitions.definition: Storage that represents data using magnetised areas on a medium, such as a hard disk or tape.
Storage read from or written to a disc using a laser, such as CD, DVD or Blu-ray.
Non-volatile electronic storage that retains data without power and has no moving parts, such as an SSD or USB drive.

points: Magnetic hard disks offer high capacity and low cost per unit of storage, but have moving parts, can be damaged by shock and are generally slower than SSDs.
Magnetic tape is inexpensive for large backups and archival storage but has slow sequential access, so locating an individual file can take time. They need to be defragmented.
Optical discs are removable, portable and useful for distributing or archiving data; read-only discs cannot be altered after manufacture.
Optical media generally has lower capacity and slower access than hard disks or SSDs, and discs can be scratched or damaged.
Flash storage is fast, compact, quiet and resistant to physical shock because it has no moving parts.
Flash devices cost more per unit of capacity than magnetic disks and have a limited number of write cycles; data recovery can be difficult after failure.

Choose a type by considering capacity, access speed, portability, durability, rewrite needs, longevity and cost; for example, SSD for fast portable computing, tape for bulk backup. A hybrid approach may be used, e.g. SSD for active data and HDD for bulk storage.

title: Flipped - RAM and ROM
hints: Candidates need to understand the purpose of ROM and RAM within a computer system, their characteristics, and the role they play in the running of a range of different computers e.g. mobile devices, embedded systems etc.

definitions.definition: Random access memory: volatile read/write main memory holding programs and data **currently** in use.
Read-only memory: non-volatile memory that retains its contents without power and stores the bootstrap (initial boot-up instructions).
Memory that loses its contents when power is removed.

points: The operating system and currently running programs/data are loaded into RAM so the CPU can access them quickly.
RAM is volatile and writable; increasing RAM can allow more programs/data to be held without relying as much on slower secondary storage.
ROM retains its contents when the device is switched off and is used for essential startup instructions or embedded firmware.
ROM contents are generally not changed during normal operation, although some forms can be updated eg through a firmware update.
A computer needs both: ROM provides instructions to start the system, while RAM provides working space for software and data.
In mobile devices and embedded systems, ROM/flash stores firmware and RAM holds the operating system, application code and active data; capacity and power use are important design constraints.

title: Flipped - Virtual storage
hints: Candidates need to understand why there is a need for virtual storage, how virtual storage works and the benefits and drawbacks of using virtual storage.
Virtual storage is storage that may appear to be local but is physically located elsewhere on the network/remotely/in the cloud.

definitions.definition: Storage presented to a user or system as if it were local, although the data is physically held elsewhere, such as on a network or in the cloud.
A service that stores data on remote servers accessed over a network, typically the internet.
Keeping local and remote copies of data consistent by transferring changes between them.

points: Virtual storage is useful when local devices have limited capacity or users need access to files from different devices or locations.
A client sends storage requests over a network; a remote server stores and retrieves the data, making it appear as part of the user's available storage.
Remote storage can provide scalable capacity, centralised backup and collaboration without installing a large local drive.
Access depends on network availability and bandwidth; slow or unavailable connections can delay or prevent access.
Users may face subscription costs, provider limits or service outages, and data must be protected against unauthorised access.
Privacy, security, data location and reliance on the service provider should be considered; encryption and access controls can reduce risk.
Local copies or synchronisation can improve offline access, but users must manage conflicts and avoid treating synchronisation as a complete backup.

title: Flipped - Need for operating systems
hints: Candidates need to have an understanding of why an operating system is required, along with the different tasks it performs within a computer system (e.g. resource management, file management, interrupt handling, security, providing a platform for software to run, providing a user interface and providing utilities).

definitions.definition: System software that manages computer hardware/resources and provides services and an interface for users and applications.
Allocating and coordinating resources such as processor time, memory and input/output devices among programs and users.
The means by which a user interacts with a computer system, such as a command-line or graphical interface.

points: An OS provides a platform and common services so application programs can run without each program controlling hardware directly.
It manages processor time and schedules processes so multiple programs can share the CPU.
It allocates and manages main memory, including tracking which processes use each area.
It organises files and directories, controlling how data is stored, retrieved and protected.
It manages input/output devices, often through device drivers, and handles interrupts from hardware or software.
It provides security features such as user accounts, authentication and permissions to restrict access.
It provides a user interface and may include utilities for tasks such as file management, configuration and system maintenance.

title: Flipped - Paging, segmentation and virtual memory
hints: Candidates need to understand how operating systems manage memory.
They need to understand the need for, purpose and function of paging to divide memory into usable fixed-size pages and how this aids in the transfer of memory for example virtual memory.
Candidates need to understand what is meant by segmentation and how memory is divided into segments to allow access to memory.
Candidates need to understand what is meant by virtual memory and why this is needed in a computer system.
Candidates need to understand how paging is used in virtual memory, and the benefits and drawbacks of having and using virtual memory in a computer system.

definitions.definition: A memory-management method that divides virtual memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into corresponding frames.
A memory-management method that divides a program into variable-sized logical sections, such as code, data and stack.
A technique that uses secondary storage to provide the appearance of more main memory than is physically available.

points: The OS divides a process's virtual address space into fixed-size pages; physical RAM is divided into same-sized frames.
A page table maps each virtual page to a physical frame; pages need not occupy contiguous physical locations, reducing external fragmentation.
When RAM is full, the OS can move less-used pages to a backing store (swap/page file) and load a required page into RAM.
If the requested page is absent, the OS is responsible for locating it on secondary storage, select space (possibly evicting another page), load it and update the mapping.
Segmentation divides memory into variable-sized logical units; segment tables can record each segment's base and limit and support protection/sharing.
Virtual memory lets larger programs or more processes run than would fit in RAM and improves memory utilisation, but disk access is much slower than RAM.
Frequent use of virtual memory can cause thrashing and severe slowdown; virtual memory also needs backing-store space and adds OS management overhead.

title: Flipped - Interrupts
hints: Candidates need to understand the purpose of interrupts within a computer system, why an interrupt might be generated and what happens within the CPU and memory in order to call an interrupt service routine.

definitions.definition: A signal/event that requests the processor's attention and temporarily diverts it from its current program.
A routine that handles a particular interrupt condition.
The code or mechanism that identifies an interrupt and transfers control to the appropriate ISR.

points: Interrupts can be generated by hardware (for example an I/O device or timer) or software (for example an exception or system call).
Interrupts allow the CPU to respond to events without continually polling every device, improving processor efficiency.
The CPU completes or safely suspends the current instruction, then saves relevant state such as the PC and status/register values, often on a stack.
The interrupt source/priority is identified, and the address of the appropriate ISR is obtained from an interrupt vector/table.
The PC is set to the ISR address and the ISR runs to service the event, such as reading device data or acknowledging a timer.
The ISR restores saved state and executes a return-from-interrupt instruction; the CPU resumes the interrupted program.
Interrupt masking or priority can control which requests are handled, preventing inappropriate interruption during critical operations.

title: Flipped - Scheduling
hints: Candidates need to understand the need for scheduling of tasks by an operating system and the benefits that scheduling brings.
Candidates need to understand that there are different scheduling algorithms, with each having benefits and drawbacks for tasks with specific characteristics.
Candidates need to understand how the following scheduling algorithms work; round robin, first come first served, multi-level feedback queue, shortest job first and shortest remaining time.

definitions.definition: The OS decision about which ready process/task receives processor time and when.
A fixed maximum period for which a process may run before round-robin scheduling moves to another process.
Scheduling in which the OS can interrupt a running process to give the CPU to another process.

points: Scheduling shares the CPU between processes, improves responsiveness and utilisation, and helps meet priorities or deadlines.
First come, first served (FCFS) runs ready processes in arrival order; it is simple and fair by arrival but a long task can delay short tasks (convoy effect).
Round robin gives each ready process a time quantum in turn; it is responsive for interactive users, but context switching adds overhead and quantum choice matters.
Shortest job first (SJF) selects the process with the shortest total expected CPU burst; it can minimise average waiting time but requires burst estimates and can starve long jobs.
Shortest remaining time (SRT) is pre-emptive SJF: the running process can be displaced when a process with a shorter remaining time becomes ready.
A multi-level feedback queue uses several priority queues; processes can move between queues based on behaviour or time used, favouring interactive jobs but risking starvation of low-priority jobs.
No algorithm is best for every workload: compare response time, waiting/turnaround time, fairness, throughput, starvation risk and scheduling overhead.

title: Flipped - Types of operating system
hints: Candidates need to understand the different (and often overlapping) classifications of operating systems (distributed, embedded, multi-tasking, multi-user and real time), including the key features of each.
They should be able to recommend (and justify) a type of operating system for a given scenario.

definitions.definition: An OS/system arrangement that manages resources across connected computers so they can work together as a system.
An OS designed for a dedicated device with specific functions and often constrained resources.
An OS that allows multiple processes to make progress by sharing processor time.
An OS that supports multiple users accessing system resources, often concurrently, with separate accounts and permissions.
An OS designed to respond to events within defined timing constraints.

points: A distributed OS is suitable when networked machines must share processing, data or resources; network delay and failures must be managed.
An embedded OS is appropriate for a dedicated device such as a controller or appliance; it is often compact and tailored to limited hardware.
A multitasking OS schedules processes so several applications appear to run at once; it is suited to general-purpose computers.
A multi-user OS supports concurrent users and must manage accounts, permissions, resource allocation and isolation; it suits shared servers.
A real-time OS provides predictable response within deadlines; it is suited to control or monitoring where late output may be incorrect or unsafe.
Classifications can overlap: a real-time OS may also be embedded, and a multi-user server may be multitasking and distributed.
Choose by scenario requirements: timing guarantees, dedicated function, number of users, concurrency, available hardware and networked resource sharing.

title: Flipped - BIOS
hints: Candidates need to understand the role of the BIOS in a computer system, and the steps that the BIOS goes through to start a computer.

definitions.definition: Basic Input/Output System: firmware that initialises hardware and starts the boot process on a computer.
Power-on self-test: startup checks that test and initialise essential hardware.
A program that locates and loads the operating system kernel into memory and transfers control to it.

points: When power is applied, the CPU begins executing firmware stored in non-volatile memory (traditionally BIOS; modern systems commonly use UEFI firmware).
The firmware performs POST, checking and initialising essential hardware such as memory, processor and peripherals; errors may be reported.
Firmware identifies a bootable device using the configured boot order, such as an internal drive or removable device.
A bootloader is loaded from the boot device and locates the operating system kernel.
The bootloader loads the kernel into RAM and transfers control to it; the OS then initialises drivers and services and presents a usable system.
Firmware settings can configure hardware and boot options; they must be stored independently of normal RAM to be available at startup.

title: Flipped - Device drivers
hints: Candidates need to understand what is meant by ‘device drivers’ and why they are needed for communication between hardware and the operating system.

definitions.definition: System software that enables an operating system to communicate with and control a particular hardware device.
Hiding device-specific details behind a consistent interface used by software.
A hardware device connected to a computer, such as a printer, keyboard or storage device.

points: Different devices can use different control commands and data formats, so the OS needs a suitable driver to operate them.
A driver translates OS requests into device-specific commands and can return status or data from the hardware to the OS.
Drivers let applications and the OS use a common interface rather than requiring each program to understand every device model.
A driver is generally specific to an operating system and device or device family; an incompatible or outdated driver may prevent correct operation.
Drivers may be supplied with the OS or installed by a device manufacturer; updates can add compatibility or fix faults.

title: Flipped - Virtual machines
hints: Virtual machines, any instance where software is used to take on the function of a machine, including executing intermediate code or running an operating system within another.

Candidates should be able to describe what is meant by a virtual machine, how they can be used to execute intermediate code, how they can be used to run a software driven machine inside a physical machine and the benefits and drawbacks of each approach.

definitions.definition: A software-created environment that behaves like a computer or machine and can run an operating system or program.
Software/firmware that creates and manages virtual machines and allocates physical resources to them.
A platform-independent or virtual-machine instruction representation produced between source code and native machine code.

points: A virtual machine can be an abstract machine used to execute intermediate code, such as bytecode, through an interpreter or runtime environment.
The same intermediate program can run on different hardware if each platform provides a compatible virtual machine/runtime.
A VM can also emulate a complete computer, allowing a guest operating system to run inside a host computer under a hypervisor.
Running multiple guest OSs can isolate environments, support testing and run software for another OS without separate physical computers.
VMs use host CPU, memory and storage; virtualisation can add performance overhead and resource contention compared with running directly on hardware.
A VM may require significant memory/storage and careful configuration; a failure or compromise in the host/hypervisor can affect guests.
Intermediate-code VMs improve portability and isolation, but require a runtime and may be slower than compiled native code.

title: Flipped - The nature of applications
hints: Candidates need to understand the purpose of applications, and should have knowledge and experience of a range of different application software (for example database, word processor, web browser, graphics manipulation etc.).
Candidates should be able to recommend the use of specific and generic applications for given scenarios, justifying their use and function(s) for a scenario.

definitions.definition: Software designed to help a user perform a particular task or set of tasks.
General-purpose application software designed for use across many tasks or users.
Software developed or selected to meet the particular requirements of an organisation or task.

points: A word processor creates and edits text documents; a spreadsheet organises numerical data, performs calculations and presents results in charts.
A database management system stores structured data and supports searching, sorting, querying and reporting.
A web browser retrieves and displays web pages; graphics-manipulation software creates or edits images.
Generic software is usually readily available, lower cost and supported, but may include unnecessary features or lack a required function.
Bespoke/specialist software can match precise workflows and requirements, but development, maintenance and support can be costly and time-consuming.
Choose software by matching required tasks, features, users, compatibility, accessibility, security, cost and training needs to the scenario.
A justified recommendation should state how the application's functions meet the stated need, not merely name the software type.

title: Flipped - Utilities
hints: Candidates need to understand the purpose and role of utility software in a computer system.
Candidates should be familiar with a range of utility software (e.g. disk defragmentation, file management, device driver, system cleanup, security etc.)

definitions.definition: System software that performs maintenance, management, security or optimisation tasks for a computer system.
Reorganising fragmented file data on a magnetic disk so file parts are stored more contiguously.
Software that creates copies of data so it can be restored after loss, damage or corruption.
Software that detects, blocks or removes malicious software.

points: File-management utilities help users copy, move, rename, search for and organise files and directories.
Defragmentation can improve access on a fragmented magnetic hard disk by reducing movement between file fragments; it is generally unnecessary for SSDs.
System-cleanup utilities remove temporary or unwanted files to free storage and may help manage system resources.
Security utilities such as anti-virus/anti-malware scan files and activity, block threats and may quarantine or remove malicious files.
Backup utilities make copies to another location or medium so data can be recovered; backups should be tested and kept separate from the original.
Driver-management utilities install or update drivers that allow the OS to operate hardware devices.
Utilities support the OS and system maintenance rather than directly performing the user's main task; poorly configured cleanup/security tools can remove needed data or affect performance.

title: Flipped - Open vs closed
hints: Candidates need to be able to explain the differences between open and closed source software, the benefits and drawbacks to creator and user of each of the licensing models, and be able to recommend which is used (with justification) for a specific scenario.

definitions.definition: Software whose source code is made available under a licence that permits specified use, inspection and often modification or redistribution.
Software whose source code is not generally available to users, who use it under the restrictions of its licence.
Legal terms that specify how software may be used, copied, modified and distributed.

points: Open-source users can inspect and, where the licence permits, modify and redistribute the source; obligations differ between licences.
Open source can enable community review, customisation and collaborative improvement, but support, documentation or updates may vary by project.
Closed-source software gives the creator greater control over code, distribution and licensing, and may provide commercial support and a consistent product.
Closed-source users generally cannot inspect or modify the source and may face licence fees, vendor dependence or restrictions on copying.

Creators may earn revenue from closed licences and protect intellectual property, but must fund development and support; open-source creators may gain contributions and adoption but monetisation can be harder.
Neither model is automatically more secure or reliable; consider maintenance, transparency, support, compatibility, total cost and required customisation.

Recommend a licence model by matching scenario needs: customisable collaborative software may favour open source; controlled proprietary distribution or dedicated vendor support may favour closed source.

title: Flipped - Translators
hints: Candidates need to understand the need for translators when writing programs.

They need to have knowledge of the differences in operation of interpreters and compilers, from these they need to be able to assess the benefits and drawbacks of using each type, and recommend with justification which should be used in a specific scenario.
Candidates need to understand the role of an assembler and how it differs from interpreters and compilers.

definitions.definition: System software that converts a program from one language or representation into another, often into machine code.
A translator that converts a source program, typically as a whole, into object or executable code before it is run.
A translator that translates and executes source code statement by statement at run time.
A translator that converts assembly-language mnemonics into machine code.

points: High-level language instructions are not directly executed by the CPU, so a translator converts them into machine-understandable machine code or an intermediate form.
A compiler translates the program before execution; the resulting executable can run repeatedly without recompiling the source each time.
Compiled code generally runs quickly, but compilation takes time and errors may need to be corrected and the program recompiled.
An interpreter translates and executes one statement at a time; it can make testing/debugging interactive and portable where an interpreter exists.
Interpreted execution is generally slower and requires the interpreter at run time; an error can be reported when the relevant statement is reached.
An assembler translates mnemonic assembly instructions and symbolic addresses into machine code; it is typically close to a one-to-one mapping.
Choose based on execution speed, development/debugging needs, distribution, target platform and whether source or an executable must be supplied.

title: Flipped - Stages of compilation
hints: Candidates need to understand that there are a number of stages involved in compilation.
Candidates need to understand how lexical analysis works and how the code is converted into tokens with the removal of unnecessary elements (e.g. comments and whitespace).
Candidates need to understand how syntax errors are identified and reported at the end of the syntax analysis.
Candidates need to understand how the abstract syntax tree will be fed into the next stage of code generation, and that the object code is then created.

Candidates need to understand why optimisation is important and how the results of lexical analysis feeds into syntax analysis, and how the tokens are checked to ensure they meet during (and after) code generation.

definitions.definition: The compilation stage that reads source characters, removes or ignores irrelevant elements and groups the remaining characters into tokens.
A classified unit of source code, such as a keyword, identifier, operator or literal.
The stage that checks token order against the language grammar and constructs a structural representation, commonly an abstract syntax tree.
The compilation stage that translates the program's representation into target/object code.
Transforming code to improve properties such as execution speed or memory use while preserving its behaviour.

points: Lexical analysis scans source characters and groups them into tokens such as identifiers, keywords, operators and constants.
Whitespace and comments that do not affect meaning are removed or ignored during lexical analysis; invalid character sequences can be flagged as lexical errors.
Syntax analysis checks whether tokens follow the language grammar and builds an abstract syntax tree (AST) representing the program's structure.
Syntax errors, such as missing brackets or an invalid token sequence, are identified and reported during syntax analysis; invalid structure cannot be compiled correctly.
The AST/other intermediate representation is passed to later stages, where semantic checks may verify meaning such as types and declarations.
Code generation translates the representation into target machine/object code; the compiler checks that operations and operands can be generated appropriately.
Optimisation improves generated code, for example by removing redundant operations or improving execution efficiency, while preserving the program's meaning.
Object code may be combined with library code by a linker to produce an executable; compilation stages pass their output to the next stage.

title: Flipped - Linkers, loaders and libraries
hints: Candidates need to understand what code libraries are, how they are used and the benefits and drawbacks from using libraries.
Candidates should have experience of using libraries to write programs.
Candidates should understand how libraries are used during compilation, and how linkers and loaders are used to combine the code and library code into the final executable file.

definitions.definition: A collection of pre-written, reusable routines or modules that a program can call to perform common tasks.
A program that combines compiled object code with required library routines and resolves references between them to produce an executable.
An operating-system utility that places an executable into main memory, prepares it to run and transfers control to it.
Including the required library code in the executable at build time.
Loading or connecting a shared library at run time rather than copying all its code into the executable.

points: A programmer calls a library routine through its documented interface instead of implementing the same functionality from scratch.
Libraries save development time, reduce duplicated code and can provide well-tested, optimised functionality.
A library may be unavailable, incompatible, poorly documented, insecure or impose licensing/version constraints.
During compilation, source code is translated into object code; unresolved library routine references are handled by the linker.
A linker resolves external symbols and combines the necessary object and library code into an executable file.
With static linking the executable is larger, but it does not need the library to be installed separately at run time.
Dynamic linking can reduce executable size and allow shared library updates, but a missing or incompatible library can prevent execution.
The loader allocates/sets up memory for the executable and its dependencies, then starts the program at its entry point.

title: Flipped - Development methodologies
hints: Candidates need to understand the following models that can be followed to produce a software system; the waterfall lifecycle, agile methodologies (specifically extreme programming); the spiral model and rapid application development).
Candidates need to understand the tasks, processes, benefits and drawbacks of each model and the similarities and differences between each.
They need to understand where each model is most suitable to use, and be able to justify the use in a situation.

definitions.definition: A sequential development lifecycle in which each phase is completed and documented before the next phase begins.
An agile method using short iterations, frequent releases, customer involvement, pair programming and continuous testing.
An iterative lifecycle organised into repeated cycles that identify objectives, assess risks, develop and evaluate a solution.
An iterative method that uses prototypes, reusable components and intensive user feedback to deliver software quickly.
An early, incomplete model of a system used to explore requirements or obtain feedback.

points: Waterfall phases commonly include requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance.
Waterfall is suitable when requirements are stable and well understood; its clear stages and documentation aid control, but changes late in development are costly.
XP divides work into short iterations with frequent working releases and continuous customer feedback; it adapts well to changing requirements.
XP practices such as pair programming and frequent testing can improve code quality, but require continual customer/team availability and discipline.
The spiral model explicitly analyses risks at each cycle, making it appropriate for large, complex or high-risk projects; risk analysis adds time and cost.
RAD rapidly builds and refines prototypes with users, making it useful when interfaces and requirements need quick clarification.
RAD can deliver quickly and improve user fit, but depends on skilled teams and user availability and may sacrifice documentation or suitability for very large systems.
All four models involve requirements, design, implementation and testing, but differ in iteration, risk management, user involvement and tolerance of change.

title: Flipped - Writing & following algorithms
hints: Candidates need to be able to write algorithms using pseudocode and/or program code.
Candidates need to be able to follow the code as shown in the OCR pseudocode guide, but are not expected to write code in this syntax.
Candidate’s code is not expected to be syntactically correct, but must use appropriate code structures.

definitions.definition: A finite, ordered set of unambiguous instructions that solves a problem or completes a task.
Instructions executed one after another in the order written.
Choosing which statements to execute according to a condition, using constructs such as IF or CASE.
Repeating a set of instructions while a condition holds or for a specified number of times.

points: An algorithm should be correct, finite, unambiguous and sufficiently efficient for its intended inputs.
Use variables to store and update values; initialise them before relying on their contents.
A condition evaluates to Boolean true or false and controls selection or loop continuation.
A count-controlled loop repeats a known number of times; a condition-controlled loop repeats until a condition changes.
Check loop bounds carefully to avoid off-by-one errors and infinite loops.
A trace table records variable values and relevant conditions after each step or iteration to follow an algorithm systematically.
Pseudocode should make sequence, selection, iteration, input, output and subroutine calls clear; equivalent program code is acceptable when appropriate.
Test an algorithm with representative and boundary inputs, then amend it if the trace or output reveals an error.

title: Flipped - Test strategies

definitions.definition: Testing an individual procedure, function, module or other small component in isolation.
Testing combined components to check that their interfaces and interactions work correctly.
Testing the complete integrated system against its functional and non-functional requirements.
Testing by or for the customer/users to decide whether the system meets agreed requirements and is ready for use.
Repeating tests after a change to check that previously working functionality has not been broken.

points: A test strategy plans what will be tested, how, by whom and at which development stages.
Testing components individually makes faults easier to isolate; integration testing can reveal interface and data-flow errors.
System testing checks the complete system, including interactions with its environment, against its specification.
Acceptance testing confirms suitability for users and may use realistic tasks and data; users or the client should be involved.
Black-box testing checks outputs against inputs and requirements without examining internal code.
White-box testing uses knowledge of the code to exercise statements, branches or paths; it can expose untested logic but does not prove correctness.
Top-down integration can use stubs for unfinished lower-level modules; bottom-up integration can use drivers to call unfinished higher-level modules.
Test early and repeat relevant tests after changes; testing can reveal defects but cannot prove that a program is completely error-free.

title: Flipped - Test data & user feedback

definitions.definition: Typical, valid data that should be accepted and processed correctly.
Valid or invalid values at, just below or just above the limits of an accepted range.
Data that is invalid, out of range or of the wrong type and should be rejected or handled safely.
Testing by developers or internal testers, usually before release to external users.
Testing by selected external users in realistic conditions before full release.

points: Normal data checks that common valid inputs produce the expected outputs.
Boundary values are important because errors often occur at the limits; for a range 1 to 10, test 0, 1, 10 and 11.
Erroneous data checks that validation rejects unsuitable input and gives an appropriate response rather than crashing or corrupting data.
Use a range of test cases, including extreme and unusual valid values, and record expected and actual results.
User feedback can identify usability problems, missing requirements and behaviours developers did not anticipate.
Alpha testing gives the development team early feedback in a controlled setting; beta testing gives feedback from real users and environments.
Acceptance testing asks users or the client to judge whether agreed requirements and practical needs are met.
Feedback should be collected systematically, prioritised, and used to make changes followed by retesting.

title: Flipped - Programming paradigms
hints: Need for and characteristics of a variety of programming paradigms.

Candidates need to understand that there are a variety of types of programming paradigms such as procedural, OOP, low-level, and that each has its strengths and weaknesses in specific scenarios, topics or areas.

definitions.definition: A general style or approach to structuring and expressing a program.
A paradigm that organises a program as ordered instructions and procedures or functions operating on data.
A paradigm that structures a program around objects combining state and operations, commonly using classes, encapsulation and inheritance.
A language closely related to processor instructions, such as machine code or assembly, with little abstraction from hardware.

points: Procedural programming is well suited to clearly ordered tasks and algorithms; procedures support reuse, but shared global data can make large programs harder to maintain.
Object-oriented programming models entities as objects and can support modularity and reuse; it may add complexity for small or simple tasks.
Low-level languages allow precise control of hardware and can be efficient, but are harder to write, debug and maintain and are often processor-specific.
High-level languages provide greater abstraction and are generally easier to develop and maintain, though they offer less direct hardware control.
A declarative approach describes the desired result or rules rather than giving every execution step; SQL is an example of a declarative language.
Different paradigms can be combined in one language or program; the best choice depends on problem, performance, maintainability and available expertise.
A paradigm influences how data and operations are represented, how a solution is decomposed and how code is reused.
No paradigm is universally best: justify a choice by linking its strengths and limitations to the scenario.

title: Flipped - Procedural languages
hints: Candidates need to have knowledge and experience of using a procedural programming language for example Python, VB.NET etc.

Candidates need to be experienced in using procedural programming features such as (but not limited to) variables, constants, selection, iteration, sequence, subroutines, string handling, file handling, Boolean and arithmetic operators.
Candidates need to be able to read, trace, amend and write procedural program code.

definitions.definition: A named block of statements that performs a task and can be called from elsewhere in a program.
A named subroutine that returns a value to the calling code.
Conditional execution of one or more alternatives, for example with IF…ELSE.
Repeated execution of statements using a loop such as FOR or WHILE.

points: Procedural programs commonly use sequence, selection, iteration and subroutines to structure instructions.
Variables store values that can change; constants represent values intended not to change during execution.
Use suitable data types, meaningful identifiers and initial values so operations behave as intended.
Boolean operators AND, OR and NOT combine or reverse conditions; arithmetic operators calculate numeric results.
Subroutines divide a solution into manageable reusable tasks and can receive parameters; functions return results.
String handling includes joining, comparing, measuring and extracting characters or substrings.
File handling allows data to persist beyond a program run by opening, reading or writing, and closing files.
To trace or amend procedural code, follow statement order, update variable values and evaluate each condition and loop carefully.

title: Flipped - Assembly language and LMC language
hints: Candidates need to have an understanding of the purpose and need for assembly language.
They need to be familiar with the instructions given in Appendix 5d.
They should be able to read, write, trace and amend programs written in the Little Man Computer language.

definitions.definition: A low-level language using mnemonic instructions that correspond closely to machine instructions and are translated by an assembler.
System software that translates assembly mnemonics and operands into machine code.
A simplified model of a computer used to learn assembly-style instructions, memory and processor operation.
A CPU register used to hold values being processed and intermediate arithmetic results.

points: Assembly provides symbolic mnemonics for machine operations and is easier for a programmer to read than binary machine code.
Assembly is processor-specific, requires detailed hardware knowledge and is more difficult to write and maintain than a high-level language.
LMC instructions include INP and OUT for input/output, LDA to load the accumulator, STA to store it, ADD and SUB for arithmetic, and HLT to stop.
LMC control instructions include BRA for an unconditional branch, BRZ for branching when the accumulator is zero and BRP for branching when it is non-negative.
DAT reserves a memory location and can initialise it with a value; labels identify instruction or data addresses.
The fetch-decode-execute cycle uses the program counter to identify the next instruction, fetches it, decodes it and executes it.
Trace an LMC program by tracking the program counter, current instruction, accumulator, memory values and any input/output.
Programs use branches to implement selection and loops; incorrect branch targets or conditions can cause wrong results or non-termination.

title: Flipped - Addressing memory
hints: Candidates need an understanding of addressing, which should be integrated with assembly language.
Candidates should have experience of using immediate, direct, indirect and indexed addressing in the writing, reading and tracing of programs written in assembly language.

definitions.definition: The method an instruction uses to specify where its operand is found or how it is obtained.
The operand value is included directly in the instruction.
The instruction contains the memory address of the operand.
The instruction refers to a location that contains the address of the operand.
An effective address is calculated by adding an index value to a base address.

points: With immediate addressing, the value is available in the instruction; it is not a memory address to dereference.
With direct addressing, the address field identifies the memory location holding the operand.
With indirect addressing, the first referenced memory location holds the effective address of the operand, requiring an extra memory access.
Indexed addressing is useful for accessing elements in arrays or tables by adding an element offset to a starting address.
Addressing modes affect instruction meaning and can influence code size and the number of memory accesses.
In assembly tracing, distinguish an operand value from an address; follow each indirection or address calculation explicitly.
The processor uses registers such as the program counter, accumulator and index register together with main memory to access instructions and data.
Choose an addressing mode that matches the data layout and operation; for example, indexed addressing suits sequential array elements.

title: Flipped - Object-oriented languages
hints: Candidates need to understand object-oriented code (as specified in the pseudocode guide).
They need to have an understanding of classes, objects, attributes and methods.
They need to understand the difference between private and public attributes and methods.
Candidates need to understand encapsulation and the use of get and set methods to access private attributes.
Candidates need to understand the purpose and principles of inheritance.
Candidates need to have an understanding of polymorphism and how it can be used within a program.
Candidates need to be able to read, trace, amend and write code that makes use of these object-oriented techniques.

definitions.definition: A definition or template specifying the attributes and methods that objects of that type have.
An instance of a class with its own attribute values and access to the class's methods.
Bundling data and methods in an object and controlling access to its internal state.
A mechanism by which a subclass derives attributes and methods from a superclass and can extend or override them.
The ability to use a common interface or method call with objects of different classes, with behaviour appropriate to each object's type.

points: Attributes store an object's state; methods define operations it can perform.
A public member can be accessed by code outside the class, whereas a private member is restricted to the class (or defined access scope).
Private attributes protect object state; public methods provide controlled interaction with an object.
Getter and setter methods retrieve or update private attributes and can validate values before changing state.
Inheritance promotes reuse and represents an is-a relationship; a subclass can add members or override inherited behaviour.
Polymorphism allows the same method call or interface to produce different behaviour for different object types.
Classes can be instantiated to create multiple objects, each with its own attribute values.
When tracing object-oriented code, track the object's class, attribute state, method calls and any overridden method selected.

title: Flipped - Introduction to programming part 1 - Program flow
hints: Candidates need to have knowledge and experience of using a procedural programming language for example Python, VB.NET etc.

Candidates need to be experienced in using procedural programming features such as (but not limited to) variables, constants, selection, iteration, sequence, subroutines, string handling, file handling, Boolean and arithmetic operators.
Candidates need to be able to read, trace, amend and write procedural program code.

definitions.definition: The order in which a program's statements are executed, including branches and repetitions.
Execution of statements in their written order.
Choosing a path of execution based on a condition.
Repeating statements while a condition is true or for a specified count.

points: A program normally begins at its entry point and executes sequential statements until it reaches a branch, loop, call or termination.
IF…ELSE selects between alternative paths according to a Boolean condition; CASE can select among several alternatives.
A FOR loop is commonly used when the number of repetitions is known; WHILE or REPEAT loops suit condition-controlled repetition.
A subroutine call transfers control to a procedure or function and returns to the calling point when it finishes.
Initialise variables before use and update loop-control variables so loops terminate as intended.
Trace code line by line, record variable changes and evaluate conditions to determine the exact output and final state.
Use indentation and clear control structures to make nesting and program logic understandable.
Test different branches and loop cases, including zero, one and multiple iterations where relevant.

title: Flipped - Introduction to programming part 2 - Variables & constants
hints: Candidates need to have knowledge and experience of using a procedural programming language for example Python, VB.NET etc.

Candidates need to be experienced in using procedural programming features such as (but not limited to) variables, constants, selection, iteration, sequence, subroutines, string handling, file handling, Boolean and arithmetic operators.
Candidates need to be able to read, trace, amend and write procedural program code.

definitions.definition: A named storage location whose value may change while a program runs.
A named value that is intended to remain unchanged during program execution.
A classification that determines the values a datum can hold and the operations that can be performed on it.
The region of a program in which an identifier can be accessed.

points: Variables hold inputs, intermediate results and outputs; assign a value before reading it.
Constants make fixed values explicit, reduce repeated literals and help prevent accidental changes.
Common types include integer, real, Boolean, character and string; choose a type appropriate to the data and required operations.
A Boolean stores true or false and is commonly used in conditions; a string stores a sequence of characters.
An assignment updates a variable's value; the expression on the right is evaluated before the result is stored.
Local variables are available only within their subroutine or scope; global variables can be accessed more widely and can increase coupling.
Meaningful identifier names and consistent naming conventions make code easier to understand and maintain.
Type conversion may be needed when combining values of different types; invalid conversions can cause errors or loss of precision.

title: Flipped - Introduction to programming part 3 - Procedures & functions
hints: Candidates need to have knowledge and experience of using a procedural programming language for example Python, VB.NET etc.

Candidates need to be experienced in using procedural programming features such as (but not limited to) variables, constants, selection, iteration, sequence, subroutines, string handling, file handling, Boolean and arithmetic operators.
Candidates need to be able to read, trace, amend and write procedural program code.

definitions.definition: A named, reusable block of code called to perform a defined task; it may be a procedure or function.
A subroutine that performs an operation without returning a value as its result.
A subroutine that returns a value to the code that called it.
A variable named in a subroutine definition that receives data supplied by the caller.
The result a function passes back to its calling code.

points: Subroutines break a program into smaller, manageable units and avoid duplicating code.
A call transfers control to the subroutine; after completion, execution resumes after the call.
Arguments are the actual values or variables passed in a call and correspond to the subroutine's parameters.
A function returns a result that can be assigned to a variable or used in an expression; a procedure is called for its action.
Local variables and parameters are generally limited to the subroutine's scope, reducing unintended interference.
Use descriptive names, clear parameters and a single well-defined purpose to make subroutines easier to test and reuse.
By-value parameters pass a value copy; by-reference parameters allow a subroutine to access or change the caller's variable, depending on the language.
Test a subroutine independently with representative inputs, then test how it interacts with the rest of the program.

title: Flipped - Introduction to programming part 4 - Mathematical operators
hints: Candidates need to have knowledge and experience of using a procedural programming language for example Python, VB.NET etc.

Candidates need to be experienced in using procedural programming features such as (but not limited to) variables, constants, selection, iteration, sequence, subroutines, string handling, file handling, Boolean and arithmetic operators.
Candidates need to be able to read, trace, amend and write procedural program code.

definitions.definition: The rules that determine the order in which operators in an expression are evaluated.
Division that returns only the whole-number quotient, discarding the fractional part.
An operation that returns the remainder after integer division.
A value or expression on which an operator acts.

points: Common arithmetic operators are addition, subtraction, multiplication and division; parentheses can make evaluation order explicit.
Exponentiation raises a value to a power where supported by the language.
Integer division and modulus are useful for quotient/remainder calculations, such as splitting a total into groups.
For positive integers, 17 DIV 5 gives 3 and 17 MOD 5 gives 2; exact operator symbols depend on the language.
Multiplication, division and exponentiation generally take precedence over addition and subtraction; parentheses override normal precedence.
Mixed integer and real arithmetic may produce a real result or require conversion, depending on the language.
Division by zero is undefined and should be prevented or handled through validation.
Trace arithmetic expressions in precedence order and check for truncation, rounding and data type effects.

title: Flipped - Introduction to programming part 5 - String handling
hints: Candidates need to have knowledge and experience of using a procedural programming language for example Python, VB.NET etc.

Candidates need to be experienced in using procedural programming features such as (but not limited to) variables, constants, selection, iteration, sequence, subroutines, string handling, file handling, Boolean and arithmetic operators.
Candidates need to be able to read, trace, amend and write procedural program code.

definitions.definition: An ordered sequence of characters treated as a single data value.
Joining two or more strings end-to-end to form a new string.
A consecutive portion of a string selected by position and, commonly, length.
The number of characters in a string.

points: Strings can contain letters, digits, spaces and punctuation; a digit stored as text is not automatically a number.
Concatenation joins strings, while arithmetic addition may instead add numeric values; convert types when required.
A program can access individual characters using an index, but whether indexing begins at zero or one depends on the language.
Substring operations extract a section of a string; check starting position and length to avoid out-of-range errors.
Common operations include finding length, comparing, searching, changing case, trimming spaces and replacing characters.
String comparison may be case-sensitive and may follow character encoding order, so do not assume all languages compare identically.
Input should be validated for required length, permitted characters and format before it is used.
Trace string expressions carefully, accounting for spaces, indexing rules and the result of each concatenation or extraction.

title: Flipped - Introduction to programming part 6 - File handling
hints: Candidates need to have knowledge and experience of using a procedural programming language for example Python, VB.NET etc.

Candidates need to be experienced in using procedural programming features such as (but not limited to) variables, constants, selection, iteration, sequence, subroutines, string handling, file handling, Boolean and arithmetic operators.
Candidates need to be able to read, trace, amend and write procedural program code.

definitions.definition: Program operations that open, read, write, append to and close files for persistent data storage.
A position marker indicating where the next read or write operation will occur in a file.
A condition indicating that no more data is available to read from a file.
A file mode that adds new data at the end of an existing file without replacing its current contents.

points: Files preserve data after a program terminates, unlike values held only in working memory.
A program should open a file in the correct mode, perform the required operations and close it when finished.
Read mode obtains existing data; write mode commonly creates or replaces file contents; append mode adds data to the end.
Read records or lines until EOF is reached, taking care not to process an absent record as valid data.
Writing should use the expected format and delimiters so the data can be read back correctly.
Handle errors such as a missing file, unavailable permissions, invalid data or insufficient storage.
Closing or safely releasing a file ensures buffered output is written and the resource is available to other processes.
Validate data read from a file because stored content may be incomplete, malformed or unexpected.

title: Flipped - Assembly language and LMC language
hints: Candidates need to have an understanding of the purpose and need for assembly language.
They need to be familiar with the instructions given in Appendix 5d.
They should be able to read, write, trace and amend programs written in the Little Man Computer language.

definitions.definition: Binary instructions directly understood by a processor.
A short symbolic name representing an assembly instruction, such as LDA or ADD.
A processor register containing the address of the next instruction to fetch.
The repeated processor process of fetching an instruction, decoding it and executing it.

points: An assembler translates mnemonic assembly code into machine code for a particular processor instruction set.
Assembly offers more readable symbolic instructions than machine code but remains hardware-dependent and less portable than high-level code.
In LMC, INP reads a value into the accumulator and OUT outputs the accumulator's value.
LDA loads a value from a specified location into the accumulator; STA stores the accumulator value in a specified location.
ADD and SUB update the accumulator; BRA, BRZ and BRP change the instruction sequence unconditionally, when zero, or when non-negative respectively.
The program counter normally advances to the next instruction, but a branch changes the address from which the next instruction is fetched.
DAT reserves a memory location for data; HLT ends execution. Labels can refer to instruction or data locations.
When tracing, follow input, accumulator, memory, program counter and output after each instruction; check branch conditions precisely.

title: Flipped - Lossy vs lossless
hints: Candidates need to understand the need for compression, especially when transferring data via the Internet.
Candidates need to understand the difference between lossy and lossless compression, and the benefits and drawbacks of each type.
Candidates need to be able to recommend a type of compression for a given scenario.

definitions.definition: Encoding data using fewer bits to reduce the storage space or transmission time required.
Compression from which the original data can be reconstructed exactly.
Compression that permanently removes some information, so the exact original cannot be reconstructed.
A comparison of the original data size with the compressed data size, used to express how much data has been reduced.

points: Compression reduces file size, saving storage and bandwidth and often reducing the time needed to transfer data over the Internet.
Lossless compression is appropriate when every bit must be recovered, such as program files, text, spreadsheets or many data archives.
Lossless decompression reproduces the original exactly, but usually achieves a smaller reduction than lossy compression for media.
Lossy compression discards information judged less noticeable, often achieving much smaller audio, image or video files.
Repeated lossy encoding can further reduce quality; the lost information cannot be restored by decompression.
Choose lossless for accuracy and future editing; choose lossy when smaller media files matter more than exact reconstruction.
The suitability of compression depends on file type, acceptable quality loss, storage limits and transmission requirements.
Compression and decompression add processing overhead, which may matter on devices with limited processing resources.

title: Flipped - Run length & dictionary coding
hints: Candidates need to understand how run-length encoding can reduce the size of a file for example with a text file or image.
Candidates should understand how dictionary coding works by substituting entries with a unique code.
Candidates should have practical experience of using these algorithms with small example files.

definitions.definition: A lossless method that represents a consecutive run of repeated symbols by the symbol and a count.
A lossless method that stores repeated strings or patterns once in a dictionary and replaces occurrences with codes or references.
A sequence of consecutive occurrences of the same symbol or value.
Extra data, such as counts, codes or a dictionary, that must be stored to allow compressed data to be decoded.

points: RLE replaces repeated adjacent values with a count and value; for example, AAAAA can be represented as 5A if the format defines this convention.
RLE works well for data containing long runs, such as simple images with large areas of the same colour.
RLE may make data larger when repeated values are rare because counts and markers add overhead.
A decoder reads each run count and symbol and reproduces the stated number of copies to reconstruct the original sequence.
Dictionary coding assigns codes to repeated patterns or strings; the decoder uses the same dictionary to expand each code.
Dictionary coding is effective when patterns recur, but the dictionary and code references also consume space.
For a small example, build the dictionary consistently, replace matching repeated entries and include enough information for unambiguous decoding.
Both methods can reconstruct the exact original when encoded and decoded correctly, but their effectiveness depends on the data pattern.

title: Flipped - Symmetric & asymmetric encryption
hints: Candidates should understand the need for encryption.
Candidates should understand how symmetric and asymmetric encryption work to encrypt and decrypt data.

definitions.definition: Transforming readable plaintext into ciphertext so that unauthorised people cannot understand it.
Transforming ciphertext back into readable plaintext using the appropriate key.
Encryption in which the same secret key is used to encrypt and decrypt data.
Encryption using a mathematically related public and private key pair, with different keys used for encryption and decryption.

points: Encryption protects confidentiality when data is stored or transmitted over an insecure channel; authorised recipients need the correct key.
In symmetric encryption, the sender and recipient share a secret key, which must be exchanged and kept secure.
Symmetric algorithms are generally fast and suitable for encrypting large quantities of data, but secure key distribution is difficult.
In public-key encryption, data encrypted with the recipient's public key can be decrypted with that recipient's private key.
