A public key can be shared openly, while the corresponding private key must be kept secret by its owner.
Asymmetric encryption simplifies secure key exchange but is generally slower than symmetric encryption for large data volumes.
Hybrid systems commonly use asymmetric cryptography to establish or exchange a symmetric session key, then symmetric encryption for bulk data.
Encryption alone does not guarantee integrity or prove who sent a message; additional mechanisms such as hashes or digital signatures may be needed.

title: Flipped - Hashing
hints: Candidates should understand the need for and purpose of using hashing algorithms to store data.
Candidates should be aware of different uses for hashing, such as the storing of passwords.

definitions.definition: A function that maps input data of arbitrary length to a fixed-length hash value or digest.
The fixed-length output produced when data is processed by a hash function.
Random data added to a password before hashing so identical passwords produce different stored hashes.
A situation in which two different inputs produce the same hash value.

points: A hash function is designed to be one-way: the original input should not feasibly be recovered from its hash.
A small change to input should produce a substantially different digest, helping detect accidental or deliberate changes.
Systems can store password hashes rather than plaintext passwords and compare a newly computed hash during login.
A unique salt is combined with each password before hashing to hinder precomputed lookup attacks and prevent identical passwords having identical stored hashes.
Passwords should be processed with a suitably slow, password-specific hashing method; a fast general-purpose hash alone is not adequate password storage.
A hash is not encryption: it has no decryption key and is not intended to recover the original message.
Because outputs have fixed length, collisions are possible in principle; a secure hash makes finding one computationally impractical.
Hashes can verify data integrity, but a plain hash does not by itself authenticate the sender if an attacker can replace both data and hash.

title: Flipped - Intro to Databases
hints: Candidates need to understand what is meant by a database.
Candidates should be familiar with basic database terminology such as fields, records and tables.
Candidates should know the difference between a flat file and a relational database, and be able to explain the benefits and limitations of each approach.
Candidates should know what is meant by a primary key, foreign key and secondary key and how each are used in a database.
Candidates should be able produce and follow Entity relationship diagrams which include 1:1, 1:M and M:M relationships. They should be able to identify how tables should be linked.
Candidates need to have an understanding of the need to interrogate data within a database.
Candidates should understand the purpose of indexing in a database and the benefits of using indexing to optimise the searching for data.

definitions.definition: An organised collection of related data that can be stored, searched, modified and managed.
A single data item or attribute in a database table, represented by a column.
A collection of related fields describing one entity or instance, represented by a row in a table.
A field or combination of fields that uniquely identifies each record in a table.
A field in one table that refers to a key, usually the primary key, in another table to establish a relationship.
An auxiliary structure that enables a database to locate records more quickly using selected field values.

points: A flat-file database stores data in one table or file; it is simple, but repeated data can cause duplication and update anomalies.
A relational database stores data in linked tables, reducing duplication and supporting consistent updates, but requires schema and relationship management.
A secondary key is a field used to search, sort or group records that does not necessarily uniquely identify a record.
ER diagrams show entities/tables and relationships: one-to-one (1:1), one-to-many (1:M) and many-to-many (M:M).
A 1:M relationship is commonly implemented by placing the primary key of the one-side table as a foreign key in the many-side table.
A M:M relationship is usually implemented with a linking table containing foreign keys to both related tables.
Database queries interrogate data to select records and fields that meet specified criteria.
Indexes speed searches and sorting on indexed fields, but use storage and can slow inserts, updates and deletes because the index must also be maintained.

title: Flipped - Methods of capturing databases
hints: Candidates need to have an awareness of a range of methods for capturing data (such as forms, OCR, OMR and sensors) selecting data (such as Query By Example and SQL), managing data (such as changing data by manipulating it – e.g. arithmetic functions, adding, editing, deleting the data) and exchanging data (with commons formats such as CSV and JSON).
Candidates won’t be specifically asked about any one of these methods but may be asked to discuss/justify suitable methods as part of a more open question.
Candidates need to have an understanding of the need to interrogate data within a database.
Candidates should understand the purpose of indexing in a database and the benefits of using indexing to optimise the searching for data.

Candidates need to have experience of a range of methods for capturing data (such as forms – what do they collect, what do they look like - data mining, where does the data come from, how is it collected and analysed), selecting data (such as how to produce QBEs – adding fields, tables, criteria, sorting - selecting through Boolean expressions – AND, OR, NOT), managing data (such as changing data by manipulating it – e.g. arithmetic functions - , adding, editing, deleting the data) and exchanging data (such as methods of transferring data – electronic i.e. memory stick, e-mail, and non-electronic e.g. paper based - appropriate formats for the transfer of data and communication mediums to transfer data – such as the structure, is it in a table or a list).

definitions.definition: Collecting data from its source and entering or importing it into a computer system.
A visual database query method in which users specify fields, criteria and sorting using a grid or form.
A standard language used to define, query and manipulate data in relational databases.
A plain-text format representing tabular data as records with fields separated by delimiters, commonly commas.
A text-based data-interchange format that represents structured data using objects, arrays and name-value pairs.

points: Forms guide data entry and can improve consistency through labels, input controls, required fields and validation.
OCR converts images of printed characters into editable text; OMR detects marked positions on forms; sensors capture measurements from the environment.
Data mining analyses large datasets to identify patterns, trends or relationships; results depend on data quality and appropriate interpretation.
QBE queries are built by choosing tables and fields, entering selection criteria and specifying sort order.
Boolean criteria combine conditions: AND requires all conditions, OR requires at least one, and NOT excludes matching values.
Database management includes adding, editing and deleting records and using calculations or functions to derive values.
CSV is widely supported and simple for tabular exchange but has limited support for data types and nested structures; delimiters in values must be handled correctly.
JSON supports nested, labelled data and is common for web exchange, but may be less compact and requires compatible parsing.
Choose capture, selection and exchange methods according to data type, accuracy, volume, user needs, compatibility and security; transfer may be electronic or paper-based.

title: Flipped - Normalisation
hints: Candidates should be able to use Normalisation to produce a suitable database schema and explain the benefits of doing so. They should be able to normalise up to 3NF.
Candidates should know and be able to apply the criteria for 1NF, 2NF and 3NF.

definitions.definition: Structuring relational tables to reduce unnecessary data duplication and prevent insertion, update and deletion anomalies.
A table is in 1NF when each field contains a single atomic value, with no repeating groups, and records can be uniquely identified.
A table is in 2NF when it is in 1NF and every non-key attribute depends on the whole candidate key, not just part of a composite key.
A table is in 3NF when it is in 2NF and non-key attributes depend only on the key, not on other non-key attributes.

points: Identify entities, attributes, candidate keys and relationships before splitting a large unnormalised table.
To reach 1NF, remove repeating groups and ensure each cell contains one value; assign a primary key if needed.
To reach 2NF, first satisfy 1NF, then move attributes that depend on only part of a composite key into a separate table.
To reach 3NF, first satisfy 2NF, then move attributes that depend on another non-key attribute into a separate table.
When decomposing tables, retain keys so related records can be linked using foreign keys.
Normalisation reduces duplicated data and helps prevent inconsistent updates and anomalies when records are inserted or deleted.
More tables can require extra joins in queries and make some retrievals more complex; normalisation is a design trade-off, not a goal of maximising table count.
Check each resulting table's key and functional dependencies to justify that it meets 1NF, 2NF and 3NF.

title: Flipped - SQL
hints: Candidates should have experience of using SQL to edit and modify data in a database. They should understand the need for SQL as a standard language.
Candidates should be able write and follow scripts using the SQL commands listed in appendix 5d.
Appendix 5d
Learners will be expected to be familiar with the structures below. Should any other aspects of SQL be used they will be introduced and explained in the question.
SELECT (including nested SELECTs) FROM
WHERE
LIKE
AND
OR
DELETE
INSERT
DROP
JOIN (Which is equivalent to INNER JOIN, there is no expectation to know about outer, left and right joins)
WILDCARDS (Learners should be familiar in the use of ‘*’ and ‘%’ as a wildcard to facilitate searching and matching where appropriate)

definitions.definition: A standard language for querying, inserting, updating and deleting data in relational databases.
An SQL statement that retrieves specified fields and records from one or more tables.
An operation that combines rows from related tables using a matching condition, typically their key fields.
A special character in a pattern that represents one or more variable characters, such as % in SQL LIKE patterns.

points: SELECT field1, field2 FROM TableName retrieves specified fields; SELECT * requests all fields.
WHERE filters records, and conditions can be combined using AND, OR and NOT; parentheses can clarify combined logic.
LIKE performs pattern matching in a WHERE clause; % represents any sequence of characters, while * is used by some systems as a wildcard for all fields in SELECT, not as the SQL LIKE wildcard.
INSERT INTO table (fields) VALUES (values) adds a record; values must match the specified fields and data types.
DELETE FROM table WHERE condition removes matching records; omitting WHERE can delete every record, so conditions must be checked carefully.
DROP TABLE removes a table and its structure as well as its data; it is not the same as deleting selected rows.
JOIN combines rows from tables using a matching key condition; an inner join returns rows with matching values in both tables.
A nested SELECT places one query inside another, often using the inner query's result as a condition for the outer query.
SQL standardisation allows similar commands to be used across relational database systems, although some syntax and features vary between implementations.

title: Flipped - Referential Integrity
hints: Candidates need to understand what is meant by referential integrity, and why this is desirable in a database.

definitions.definition: A rule ensuring that every foreign key value in a table matches an existing primary key value in the related table, so relationships between tables stay consistent.
A field (or fields) that uniquely identifies each record in a table.
A field in one table that is the primary key of another table, used to link the two tables.
A record whose foreign key refers to a record that no longer exists in the related table.

points: Referential integrity stops a foreign key from referring to a non-existent primary key.
Without it, deleting a record in the parent table could leave orphan records in the child table.
Example: an order cannot be added for a CustomerID that does not exist in the Customer table.
A parent record cannot be deleted while child records still refer to it, unless deletion is cascaded.
A primary key value cannot be changed if related records exist, unless the update is cascaded.
Cascade delete/update automatically applies changes to related records to keep data consistent.
It keeps data accurate and consistent and avoids queries returning incomplete or missing data.
It is enforced by the database management system (DBMS) when relationships are defined.

title: Flipped - Transaction Processing
hints: Candidates should understand what is meant by transaction processing, and scenarios where transaction processing takes place.
Candidates should understand the problems that arise from transaction processing, and how these can be overcome.
Candidates should understand the ACID rules for transaction processing, and why databases should be built to these standards.
Candidates should understand how record locking prevents the overriding of data and understand how record locking takes place.

definitions.definition: A sequence of database operations that must be treated as a single unit of work: either all of it completes or none of it does.
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the four properties a database must guarantee for reliable transaction processing.
Preventing other users or processes from accessing or editing a record while it is being updated by one user.
Undoing the partial changes of a failed transaction to return the database to its previous consistent state.
When two users edit the same record at the same time, one update overwrites the other and data is lost or becomes inconsistent.

points: Examples of transaction processing: online banking transfers, airline/theatre seat booking and online shopping.
Problem: two users updating the same record at once can cause lost updates and inconsistent data (for example a seat double-booked).
Atomicity: all parts of a transaction succeed or none do, otherwise it is rolled back.
Consistency: a transaction must take the database from one valid state to another, obeying all rules and constraints.
Isolation: concurrent transactions must not interfere, so the result is as if they ran one after another.
Durability: once a transaction is committed it is permanently stored, even after a system failure.
Record locking: when a record is accessed for update it is locked; others wait or have read-only access until it is released.
Locking prevents overwriting but can cause delays, and deadlock if two transactions each wait for the other's lock.
Other methods: serialisation of transactions and timestamp ordering.

title: Flipped - Network characteristics & protocols
hints: Characteristics of networks and the importance of protocols and standards.
Candidates need to understand the definition and purpose of a network.

Candidates need to understand the purpose of, and importance of using protocols. They should be able to discuss examples of protocols that may be used in a network/the internet (but will not be asked to recall information about any specific protocol).
Candidates should understand the term standard and the purpose and need for standards in a network (or any situation where data is transferred).

definitions.definition: Two or more computing devices connected together so that they can communicate and share data and resources.
An agreed set of rules governing how data is transmitted and received between devices, such as format, speed, error checking and addressing.
An agreed specification that manufacturers and developers follow so that hardware and software from different sources work together.
The exchange of signals between devices to establish communication parameters before data transfer begins.

points: Purpose of a network: share files, hardware (printers), internet connections and applications, and allow communication.
Protocols define data format, packet structure, addressing, speed, error detection and how communication starts and ends.
Protocols let different makes of device and different systems communicate successfully.
Examples: HTTP/HTTPS (web pages), FTP (file transfer), SMTP/POP3/IMAP (email), TCP/IP, and UDP.
Standards ensure compatibility and interoperability between devices from different manufacturers.
Standards allow competition and a wider choice of products, and make components replaceable.
Without standards and protocols, data could be misinterpreted or devices unable to communicate.
Standards apply to any situation where data is transferred, for example Ethernet, Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) and file formats.

title: Flipped - TCP/IP, DNS & protocol layers
hints: Candidates need to understand the purpose and benefits of layering protocols, particularly within the TCP/IP stack.
Candidates need to know the different layers within the TCP/IP stack and the purpose of each.
Candidates need to understand how data is transmitted on the Internet, the use of IP addresses and packets in the transfer of data. (NB Candidates are not expected to be familiar with the OSI model).
Candidates need to understand how the Domain Name System is used to find the IP of a URL is found.

definitions.definition: A four-layer model of network protocols: application, transport, network (internet) and link (network access).
A unique numerical address that identifies a device on a network and is used to route packets to it.
A small unit of data containing a header (including source and destination IP addresses, packet number and TTL), the payload and error checking data.
A distributed system of servers that translates domain names/URLs into IP addresses.
Dividing network communication into separate layers, each with its own specific function and protocols.

points: Application layer: provides protocols such as HTTP, SMTP and FTP for the user's software to use.
Transport layer (TCP): splits data into packets, numbers them, and reassembles and checks them at the destination.
Network/internet layer (IP): adds source and destination IP addresses and routes packets across networks.
Link/network access layer: handles the physical transmission using MAC addresses and the hardware (NIC, cable, Wi-Fi).
Benefits of layering: each layer is independent so one can change without affecting others, it breaks a complex problem into manageable parts and promotes standards and interoperability.
Data is split into packets, each routed independently by routers, possibly via different routes, then reassembled in order using packet numbers.
DNS: the browser asks a DNS server for the URL's IP address; if unknown the request passes to other DNS servers up the hierarchy and the IP address is returned and cached.
Data passes down the layers at the sender and up the layers at the receiver.

title: Flipped - LANs & WANs
hints: Candidates are expected to understand the terms LAN and WAN.

definitions.definition: A network covering a small geographical area, such as a building or site, usually owned and managed by one organisation.
A network covering a large geographical area, such as cities, countries or worldwide, often using leased or public telecommunications infrastructure.
The largest WAN: a global network of interconnected networks.

points: A LAN covers a small area such as a school, office or home.
A LAN is typically owned and maintained by the organisation using it, with its own cabling and hardware.
A LAN has high data transfer speeds and low cost to set up compared with a WAN.
A WAN covers a large area and connects LANs together.
A WAN usually relies on third-party infrastructure (leased lines, telephone networks, satellite) so is more expensive and slower.
Example LAN: school computer network. Example WAN: the Internet or a bank linking its branches.
WANs can use routers, switches and modems to connect LANs.
A WAN is more prone to errors and slower speeds because of distance and shared infrastructure.

title: Flipped - Packet & circuit switching
hints: Candidates need to understand the purpose, function, benefits and drawbacks of both packet and circuit switching.
Candidates need to be able to suggest packet or circuit switching for a given scenario.

definitions.definition: A method where data is split into packets that are each routed independently across the network and reassembled at the destination.
A method where a dedicated communication path is established between sender and receiver for the whole duration of the communication.
A device that forwards packets between networks using their destination IP addresses.
The delay between data being sent and being received.

points: Packet switching: data is split into packets, each with a header, and routers choose the best route for each packet.
Packets may take different routes and arrive out of order, so they are reassembled using packet numbers.
Packet switching benefits: efficient use of bandwidth, no dedicated line needed, packets can avoid congestion or failed links, and it is cheaper.
Packet switching drawbacks: packets can be lost or arrive out of order, and delay varies (jitter) so it is less suited to real-time use.
Circuit switching: a dedicated path is set up before communication, and kept open until it ends (like a traditional telephone call).
Circuit switching benefits: constant data rate, low latency, data arrives in order, and the line is secure from interference from other traffic.
Circuit switching drawbacks: line is reserved even when idle (wasteful), setup time is required, and a failure breaks the connection.
Scenario: packet switching suits web browsing, email and file downloads; circuit switching suits a continuous live call where consistent quality is needed.

title: Flipped - Network security threats
hints: Candidates need to understand that there are a range of security issues and threats involved with networked computers.
Candidates need to be aware of threats such as hackers, viruses, unauthorised access, denial of service, spyware, SQL injection, phishing and pharming.
Candidates need to know about ways of minimising, or preventing these threats for example firewalls, secure passwords, anti-virus, anti-spyware etc.

definitions.definition: An attack that floods a server or network with requests so legitimate users cannot access it.
Fraudulent emails or messages that trick users into revealing personal information or visiting fake websites.
Redirecting users from a genuine website to a fake one, for example by altering DNS data or host files, to steal their details.
Inserting malicious SQL code into an input field so that a database executes unintended commands and exposes or alters data.
Software or hardware that monitors and filters incoming and outgoing network traffic based on rules.

points: Hackers gain unauthorised access to systems to steal, alter or destroy data.
Viruses and malware are programs that replicate or damage files, and spyware secretly records user activity such as keystrokes.
Unauthorised access can be reduced by strong passwords, user access levels and authentication.
DoS attacks (often distributed, DDoS, using many computers or a botnet) overload a server with traffic.
SQL injection is prevented by input validation and sanitisation and by using parameterised queries.
Phishing is reduced by user education, spam filters and not clicking unknown links; pharming by using HTTPS and keeping DNS secure.
Anti-virus and anti-spyware software detect and remove malware, and should be kept up to date.
Firewalls block suspicious traffic, and encryption protects data in transit so it cannot be understood if intercepted.
Other measures: regular software patching, penetration testing, backups and physical security.

title: Flipped - Network hardware
hints: Candidates need to have knowledge of the hardware required to connect to and/or build a network (e.g. modem, router, cable, NIC, Wireless Access Points, hub, switch etc).
Candidates need to understand the purpose of the hardware, but are not required to understand how they physically work.

definitions.definition: A hardware component that allows a device to connect to a network, providing a MAC address.
A device that connects devices in a LAN and forwards data only to the device it is intended for, using MAC addresses.
A device that connects different networks together and forwards packets between them using IP addresses.
A device that modulates and demodulates signals, converting digital data to and from analogue signals for transmission over telephone or cable lines.
A device that allows wireless devices to connect to a wired network using Wi-Fi.

points: A hub broadcasts incoming data to all connected devices, which causes collisions and wastes bandwidth.
A switch sends data only to the intended device so is more efficient and secure than a hub.
A router connects a LAN to the internet or other networks and directs packets, often including a firewall and DHCP.
A modem connects a network to the internet via a telephone or cable line; many home routers include a modem.
A NIC (wired or wireless) is needed in every device to connect to the network.
A WAP extends a wired network to wireless devices.
Transmission media: copper cable (twisted pair, coaxial), fibre optic (fast, long distance, immune to interference) and wireless.
A gateway/router and bridges can link networks that use different protocols or segments.

title: Flipped - Client server & peer to peer
hints: Candidates need to understand the difference between a client-server and peer-to-peer network.
Candidates need to know the benefits and drawbacks of each type of network and be able to recommend one for a given scenario.

definitions.definition: A network where client computers request services and resources from a central server that manages them.
A network where each computer is equal, sharing its own resources directly with other computers without a central server.
A computer that provides services, such as file storage, email or web pages, to clients.
A computer or device that requests services from a server.

points: Client-server benefits: centralised management, backup, security and access control; easier to monitor and update.
Client-server drawbacks: server is expensive and needs a specialist administrator; if the server fails, clients lose access; heavy traffic can slow it.
Peer-to-peer benefits: cheap and simple to set up, no dedicated server or specialist needed, and no single point of failure.
Peer-to-peer drawbacks: harder to secure and back up, files are stored on different machines, and performance depends on each peer.
In P2P each device acts as both client and server, for example file sharing with BitTorrent.
Recommend client-server for large organisations such as a school needing central security and file storage.
Recommend peer-to-peer for a small home or small office network with few computers and little need for central control.
Client-server examples: web servers, email servers, and school networks with logins.

title: Flipped - HTML, CSS and JavaScript
hints: Candidates need to understand the purpose of HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
Candidates should have experience of writing webpages using HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
Candidates need to be able to recognise the code in Appendix 5d, and be able to read, write, amend and interpret code using HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

definitions.definition: HyperText Markup Language: a markup language that defines the structure and content of a web page using tags.
Cascading Style Sheets: a language that defines the presentation of web page elements, such as colours, fonts and layout.
A scripting language run in the browser that adds interactivity and dynamic behaviour to web pages.

A marker in HTML, usually in pairs such as

and

, that tells the browser how to treat the content.

points: HTML structures content with elements such as headings (h1), paragraphs (p), links (a), images (img), lists, tables and forms.
Forms use input elements to collect data, with attributes such as type, name and id.
CSS selects elements by tag, class (.) or id (#) and sets properties like colour, font-size and margin.
CSS can be inline, internal in a style element, or external in a linked .css file; external is best for consistency.
Separating content (HTML) from style (CSS) makes sites easier to maintain and restyle.
JavaScript can respond to events (such as onclick), validate form input, and change page content using the DOM.
JavaScript uses variables, selection, iteration and functions like other programming languages.
JavaScript is included with a script element, either inline or from an external .js file.

title: Flipped - Search engine indexing
hints: Candidates should understand how and why search engine results are indexed.

definitions.definition: A program that finds web pages matching a user's search terms and returns them as a ranked list of results.
A program that automatically follows hyperlinks from page to page, collecting data about each page.
A large database of keywords mapped to the web pages that contain them, used for fast retrieval of search results.
HTML information in the head of a page, such as keywords and description, that describes the page to search engines.

points: Web crawlers visit pages by following links and send content back to be processed.
Pages are analysed for keywords, titles, headings, meta tags and links, and the data is stored in the index.
The index allows fast searching without scanning the whole web at query time.
The index is updated regularly by recrawling pages so results stay current.
When a user searches, the search terms are matched against the index to find relevant pages.
Results are then ordered using algorithms such as PageRank and relevance of the content.
Pages can be excluded from crawling using a robots.txt file.
Indexing is needed because the web is far too large to search in real time.

title: Flipped - PageRank algorithm
hints: Candidates understand how PageRank ranks the results of search engine results.
Candidates should understand how page rank works at a high level but are not expected to be able to code the algorithm.

definitions.definition: An algorithm that ranks web pages by importance, based on the number and quality of links pointing to them.
A hyperlink on another page that points to a given page.
A probability (typically about 0.85) that a user randomly following links continues to the next page rather than jumping to a random page.
A hyperlink on a page that points to another page.

points: A page with more inbound links is considered more important and ranks higher.
Links from highly ranked pages are worth more than links from low-ranked pages.
A page's rank is shared out between the pages it links to, so a page with many outbound links gives less to each.
It is modelled as a random surfer clicking links; PageRank is the probability the surfer ends up on a page.
The damping factor allows for the surfer getting bored and jumping to a random page.
Ranks are calculated iteratively, with each pass using the previous values, until they stabilise.
PageRank is one of many factors used to order search results.
It helps counter manipulation, since links from reputable pages carry more weight than many links from poor ones.

title: Flipped - Server and client side processing
hints: Candidates need to understand the difference between server and client side processing, and should be aware of examples (for example Javascript code vs PHP code) of processing on both sides.
Candidates should be aware of the benefits and drawbacks of both types of processing.

definitions.definition: Code that is executed on the web server, with only the resulting output (usually HTML) sent to the client's browser.
Code that is downloaded and executed by the user's browser on their own computer.
A computer that hosts a website and responds to requests from clients.

points: Client-side examples: JavaScript, HTML and CSS; typically used for form validation, animations and interactive content.
Server-side examples: PHP, Python, ASP.NET; used for database access, user authentication and processing orders.
Client-side benefits: reduces load on the server, gives immediate response without a network round trip, and reduces bandwidth.
Client-side drawbacks: code is visible and can be altered by users, so it is less secure; relies on the browser and device supporting it.
Server-side benefits: code is hidden from users, so it is more secure; works on any browser; can access databases directly.
Server-side drawbacks: increases load on the server, needs network round trips so is slower to respond, and the server may become overloaded.
Client-side validation is quick but should be repeated on the server because it can be bypassed.
Many sites use both: client-side for responsiveness and server-side for data handling and security.

title: Flipped - Lossy vs lossless
hints: Candidates need to understand the need for compression, especially when transferring data via the Internet.
Candidates need to understand the difference between lossy and lossless compression, and the benefits and drawbacks of each type.
Candidates need to be able to recommend a type of compression for a given scenario.

definitions.definition: Reducing the size of a file so that it uses less storage and takes less bandwidth and time to transmit.
Compression that permanently removes some data, so the original file cannot be perfectly restored.
Compression that reduces file size without losing any data, so the original can be perfectly reconstructed.
A lossless technique that replaces consecutive repeated values with a single value and a count.
A lossless technique that replaces repeated patterns of data with shorter references to entries in a dictionary.

points: Compression is needed to save storage space and to reduce transfer time and bandwidth use over the Internet.
Lossy removes data that is less noticeable to humans, for example by reducing colour depth or removing inaudible frequencies.
Lossy examples: JPEG images, MP3 audio and MPEG video.
Lossy benefits: much smaller files and faster downloads and streaming.
Lossy drawbacks: quality is permanently lost and the original cannot be recovered; repeated compression degrades quality further.
Lossless examples: PNG, GIF, ZIP and FLAC.
Lossless benefits: the exact original is restored, so it is suitable for text, program code and data where nothing can be lost.
Lossless drawbacks: files are larger than with lossy, so savings are smaller.
Recommend lossy for streaming video or web photos; lossless for documents, software and archiving.

title: Flipped – Primitive Data Types
hints: Candidates need to have an understanding of programming data types such as integer, real, Boolean, character, string etc.
Candidates need to be able to choose appropriate data types for a situation or given data.

definitions.definition: A whole number, positive or negative, with no fractional part.
A number that can have a fractional part.
A data type with only two possible values: true or false.
A single letter, digit, symbol or space.
A sequence of characters.

points: Integer example: number of students, such as 25.
Real example: a price or a height, such as 1.75.
Boolean example: whether a user is logged in (true/false).
Character example: a grade 'A'; String example: a name such as 'Alice'.
A telephone number should be stored as a string because it is not used in calculations and may have leading zeros.
Choose the type that suits the data and the operations needed, such as integers for counting and arithmetic.
Using appropriate data types saves memory, improves efficiency and allows validation.
A date can be stored as a date type or string, depending on whether date calculations are needed.

title: Flipped – Binary Positive Integers
hints: Candidates should understand how and why computers store data as binary using switches, and that a binary number can have a variety of different interpretations depending on what is being stored (e.g. numeric, text, image, sound).
Candidates should be able to convert positive whole numbers to binary and from binary to decimal/denary.

definitions.definition: A base 2 number system using only the digits 0 and 1.
A binary digit: the smallest unit of data, either 0 or 1.
A group of 8 bits.
The base 10 number system using digits 0 to 9.

points: Computers use binary because digital circuits are made from switches (transistors) that are either on (1) or off (0).
The same binary pattern can represent a number, text character, image pixel or sound sample depending on how it is interpreted.
Place values in binary double each time from the right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128.
Binary to denary: add the place values where there is a 1, for example 1011 = 8+2+1 = 11.
Denary to binary: subtract the largest place value that fits (or repeatedly divide by 2) and record 1s and 0s, for example 13 = 1101.
An 8-bit unsigned integer can store values from 0 to 255.
n bits can represent 2 to the power n different values.
Leading zeros can pad a number to a fixed width, for example 5 = 00000101.

title: Flipped – Hexadecimal Representation
hints: Candidates need to have an understanding of the purpose and potential uses of Hexadecimal for example where and why they are used instead of binary and the benefits of using Hexadecimal over alternatives such as binary.
Candidates should be able to convert denary numbers to hexadecimal and vice-versa and from binary to hexadecimal and vice-versa.

definitions.definition: A base 16 number system using the digits 0 to 9 and letters A to F, where A=10 and F=15.
A group of 4 bits, which corresponds to exactly one hexadecimal digit.
A number system with sixteen symbols, where each place value is sixteen times the one to its right.

points: One hex digit represents 4 bits, so two hex digits represent one byte.
Hex is shorter and more compact than binary and so easier for humans to read, write and remember.
Hex is less error-prone than long binary strings.
Uses: colour codes in HTML/CSS (such as #FF0000), memory addresses, MAC addresses and error codes.
Binary to hex: split into groups of four bits from the right and convert each, for example 1010 1111 = AF.
Hex to binary: convert each hex digit to 4 bits, for example 3C = 0011 1100.
Hex to denary: multiply each digit by its power of 16, for example 2F = 2x16 + 15 = 47.
Denary to hex: divide by 16 and use the quotient as the first digit and the remainder as the second, for example 255 = FF.
Computers still use binary internally; hex is only a convenient human representation.

title: Flipped – Sign & Magnitude + Two’s Complement
hints: Candidates should know how to store negative numbers using Sign and Magnitude and two’s complement.
Candidates should be able to convert denary numbers to sign and magnitude, and two’s complement – and vice-versa.

definitions.definition: A way to store signed integers in which the most significant bit is the sign (0 positive, 1 negative) and the remaining bits hold the magnitude.
A way to store signed integers in which the most significant bit has a negative place value, for example -128 in 8 bits.
The leftmost bit, which has the highest place value.

points: Sign and magnitude example in 8 bits: +5 = 00000101 and -5 = 10000101.
Sign and magnitude range in 8 bits is -127 to +127.
Sign and magnitude drawbacks: two representations of zero (+0 and -0), and arithmetic is more complicated.
Two's complement in 8 bits has place values -128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, giving a range of -128 to +127.
To convert a negative number to two's complement: write the positive binary, invert all bits, then add 1 (or keep bits up to the first 1 and invert the rest).
To convert two's complement to denary, add the place values, using -128 for the MSB, for example 11111011 = -128+64+32+16+8+2+1 = -5.
Two's complement has only one zero and allows addition and subtraction with the same circuitry.

title: Flipped – Binary Addition & Subtraction
hints: Candidates should be able to perform addition and subtraction on integer binary numbers. (These numbers could be positive or negative using two’s complement representation.)

definitions.definition: Adding binary numbers column by column using 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=10 (write 0, carry 1) and 1+1+1=11.
When the result of a calculation is too large to be stored in the available number of bits.
Subtracting a number by adding its two's complement negative.

points: Add from the right, carrying 1 to the next column when a column totals 2 or more.
To subtract, convert the number being subtracted to its negative in two's complement and add.
Example: 7 - 3 is 00000111 + 11111101 = 1 00000100; discard the carry out of the MSB to get 4.
A carry out of the leftmost bit is discarded in two's complement arithmetic.
Overflow occurs if the result is outside the range, for example 01111111 + 1 gives 10000000 (-128 in 8 bits) which is incorrect.
Overflow can be detected when two positives give a negative result or two negatives give a positive.
Check answers by converting back to denary.

title: Flipped – Character Sets
hints: Candidates should have an understanding of how characters are represented in a computer and in binary.
Candidates should understand the need for a character set and how a computer makes use of a character set.
Candidates should be aware of the ASCII and UNICODE character sets and be able to explain the differences between these and how these impact what can be stored.

Candidates should be able to use a character set, or part of a character set, to translate characters into binary and vice-versa. (Candidates are not expected to memorise any values in a character set).

definitions.definition: A defined list of characters that a computer can recognise, each with a unique binary code.
A character set using 7 bits (128 characters, with extended versions using 8 bits) to represent English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes.
A character set that assigns a code to characters from almost all of the world's writing systems, using up to 32 bits (such as UTF-8 and UTF-16).
The unique binary number assigned to a character in a character set.

points: A character set is needed because computers store only binary, so characters must be mapped to binary codes that all devices agree on.
Text is stored as a sequence of character codes, and the computer uses the character set to display them.
ASCII has 128 characters in 7 bits, which is enough for English but not for other languages.
Extended ASCII uses 8 bits for 256 characters.
Unicode uses more bits per character, so can represent many languages, symbols and emojis.
Unicode is backwards compatible with ASCII: its first 128 codes are the same.
Unicode files are larger than ASCII, since more bits are needed per character.
Codes for letters are consecutive, so if 'A' is known, 'B' is the next value; this allows conversion between characters and binary.

title: Flipped – Bitwise Manipulation & Masks
hints: Bitwise manipulation and masks: shifts, combining with AND, OR, and XOR.
Candidates should be able to perform right and left logical shifts.
Candidates should understand the effect of right and left shifts on a binary number.
Candidates should understand the purpose of using masks with bitwise operators, and should have experience of applying masks using AND, OR and XOR.

definitions.definition: Moving all the bits in a binary number left or right by a number of places, filling vacated positions with zeros.
A binary pattern used with a bitwise operator to test, set, clear or toggle selected bits of another value.
An operation giving 1 in each position only where both bits are 1; used to clear or check bits.
An operation giving 1 in each position where either bit is 1; used to set bits.
An operation giving 1 in each position where the bits are different; used to toggle bits.

points: A left shift by n places multiplies an unsigned binary number by 2 to the power n.
A right shift by n places divides by 2 to the power n, discarding the remainder.
Bits shifted out of the end are lost, and zeros are added at the other end.
Example: 00001100 shifted left once is 00011000 (12 becomes 24).
AND with a mask of 0s clears bits, and AND with 1s keeps them, so it can check whether a bit is set.
OR with a mask sets the bits where the mask has 1.
XOR with a mask flips the bits where the mask has 1, and XOR is used in simple encryption.
Example: 10110110 AND 00001111 = 00000110, keeping only the lower four bits.

title: Flipped – Floating Point Binary
hints: Candidates should have an understanding of how (positive and negative) real numbers are represented in a binary floating-point representation and should be able to convert between a denary number and a real binary number. (NB the representation used for the exam is the mantissa and exponent both represented using two’s complement.)

definitions.definition: A way of storing real numbers as a mantissa and an exponent, in the form mantissa x 2 to the power exponent.
The part of a floating point number that holds the significant digits and sign; it determines the precision.
The part that holds the power of 2 by which the mantissa is multiplied; it determines the range.
The binary equivalent of a decimal point, separating whole parts from fractional parts.

points: In the exam the mantissa and exponent are both stored in two's complement.
The mantissa is treated as a fraction with the binary point after the sign bit, for example 0.1010000.
Place values after the binary point are 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16 and so on.
To convert to denary: work out the mantissa value, then multiply by 2 to the power of the exponent (a positive exponent moves the point right; negative moves it left).
Example: mantissa 0.1100000 (0.75) with exponent 0011 (3) is 0.75 x 8 = 6.
A negative number has a mantissa beginning with 1 and is read using two's complement.
To convert denary to floating point, write the number in binary, move the binary point to just after the sign bit and set the exponent to record the shift.
More bits for the mantissa give greater accuracy; more bits for the exponent give a bigger range.

title: Flipped – Floating Point Binary Normalisation
hints: Candidates should understand the need for normalised floating-point numbers.
Candidates should be able to normalise a floating-point number.
The second video includes more worked examples.

definitions.definition: Adjusting the mantissa and exponent so that the mantissa starts 01 (positive) or 10 (negative), giving the maximum precision.
A floating point number whose mantissa has its first two bits different.
How accurately a number can be represented, determined by the number of bits in the mantissa.

points: Normalisation is needed to use the available mantissa bits as efficiently as possible and so maximise precision.
It also gives a single unique representation for each number, which makes comparison easier.
A positive normalised mantissa starts 0.1; a negative normalised mantissa starts 1.0.
To normalise, shift the mantissa left until the first two bits differ, and subtract 1 from the exponent for each left shift.
If the mantissa is shifted right, increase the exponent by 1 for each place.
Example: 0.0011000 x 2^4 normalises to 0.1100000 x 2^2.
Unnormalised numbers waste bits on leading zeros (or ones for negatives), reducing accuracy.
Normalisation does not change the value of the number.

title: Flipped – Floating Point Arithmetic
hints: Candidates should be able to perform addition and subtraction floating point arithmetic including addition and subtraction of both positive and negative numbers.

definitions.definition: Adding two floating point numbers by first making the exponents equal, then adding the mantissas and normalising the result.
Subtracting by aligning the exponents then adding the two's complement of the second mantissa, and normalising.
Shifting the mantissa of the number with the smaller exponent right, increasing its exponent, until the exponents match.

points: Step 1: compare exponents and align them to the larger one.
Step 2: shift the mantissa of the number with the smaller exponent right by the difference, keeping the sign bit by sign extension.
Step 3: add the mantissas, or for subtraction add the two's complement of the second.
Step 4: normalise the result by shifting and adjusting the exponent.
The exponent stays the same during the addition itself.
Bits shifted off the right-hand end may be lost, reducing accuracy.
Overflow in the mantissa can require a right shift and an increase in the exponent.
Check the final answer by converting back to denary.

title: Flipped - Arrays, records, lists & tuples
hints: Candidates should be able to describe what is meant by arrays (up to 3 dimensions), records, lists and tuples.
They are expected to be able recognise when they can be used and incorporate them in their programs to store data.

definitions.definition: A fixed-size, ordered data structure holding elements of the same data type, accessed by index.
A data structure made up of a fixed number of fields, which can be of different data types, grouped under one name.
An ordered, dynamic data structure that can change in size and may hold items of different types.
An ordered, immutable data structure whose contents cannot be changed once created.
An array of arrays, accessed with more than one index, such as a 2D table or 3D cube.

points: A 1D array is a simple sequence, for example names[2]; a 2D array is like a table accessed as grid[row][column].
A 3D array adds a third index, for example a set of tables accessed as data[x][y][z].
Arrays are static in size and hold a single data type, so access is fast through index.
A record groups related fields of different types, for example a student with name (string), age (integer) and fee paid (Boolean).
Records are accessed by field name, for example student.name.
Lists can grow and shrink, with items added, removed or inserted, and may be mixed type depending on the language.
Tuples are immutable, so are safer for data that must not change, such as coordinates (3, 5).
Use arrays for fixed collections of the same type, records for one entity with varied attributes, lists for changing collections and tuples for constant groups.

title: Flipped - Data structures part 1 - Linked lists
hints: Candidates need to have an understanding of the behaviour of linked-lists.
Candidates need to be able be aware of how the linked lists can be implemented.

definitions.definition: A dynamic linear data structure made of nodes, where each node stores data and a reference (pointer) to another node.
An element of a linked list containing a data value and one or more links to other nodes.
A reference to the first node in a linked list; an empty list has a null head.
A stored reference identifying the next node (and, in a doubly linked list, the previous node).

points: In a singly linked list each node links to the next node; the final node links to null. A doubly linked list has links in both directions.
Nodes need not occupy adjacent memory locations; links maintain their logical order.
A list can grow or shrink at run time, subject to available memory, without shifting all subsequent elements.
Insertion or deletion is efficient when the relevant node/link is already known: update links rather than move other values.
Finding an item by position generally requires traversal from the head, so access is sequential and takes O(n) time.
Each node requires memory for its link(s), and pointer handling makes implementation more complex than an array.
A linked list can be implemented with node objects/references or with arrays holding data and a next-index; a free-list can track unused array slots.

title: Flipped - Data structures part 2 - Graphs
hints: Candidates need to have an understanding of the behaviour of  graphs
Candidates need to be able be aware of how graphs can be implemented.

definitions.definition: A non-linear data structure consisting of vertices (nodes) connected by edges (arcs).
A node in a graph representing an entity or state.
A connection between two vertices; it may be directed or undirected and may have a weight.
Two vertices are adjacent when an edge directly connects them.

points: Graphs represent networks such as roads, social connections and computer networks; they need not have a root or a single linear order.
An undirected edge can be followed both ways; a directed edge (arc) has a specified source and destination.
A weighted graph assigns a value such as distance or cost to an edge; an unweighted graph records connection only.
An adjacency matrix stores connections in a V by V table; a cell records whether (or the weight with which) two vertices connect.
A matrix gives quick edge lookup but uses O(V²) space, even when few edges exist; for an undirected graph it is symmetric.
An adjacency list stores, for each vertex, the vertices joined to it (and optional weights); it saves space for sparse graphs but edge lookup may require a search.
A graph can be traversed using depth-first search (follow an unvisited neighbour deeply, backtrack) or breadth-first search (visit neighbours level by level), marking visited vertices to avoid loops.

title: Flipped - Data structures part 3 - Stacks & queues
hints: Candidates need to have an understanding of the behaviour of stacks & queues.
Candidates need to be able be aware of how stacks & queues can be implemented.

definitions.definition: A linear abstract data type in which the most recently added item is the first one removed (LIFO).
A linear abstract data type in which the earliest added item is the first one removed (FIFO).
The stack operation that adds an item to the top.
The queue operation that adds an item at the rear.
Overflow is attempting to add to a full bounded structure; underflow is attempting to remove from an empty one.

points: A stack is accessed at its top: push adds there and pop removes and returns the top item; peek reads it without removing it.
Stacks are used for function calls/recursion, undo operations and expression evaluation; the call stack follows LIFO order.
A queue removes from the front and adds at the rear; front/ head and rear/tail indices identify these positions.
Queues model waiting lines and are used in breadth-first search, print spooling and task scheduling.
An array stack can use a top index; an array queue can use front and rear indices, with a circular queue wrapping indices modulo capacity.
An array implementation has fixed capacity unless resized and must detect overflow/underflow; a linked implementation can grow dynamically but uses links and extra memory.
An ADT specifies operations and behaviour independently of whether it is implemented with arrays, linked nodes or another structure.

title: Flipped - Data structures part 4 - Trees
hints: Candidates need to have an understanding of the behaviour of trees.
Candidates need to be able be aware of how trees can be implemented.

definitions.definition: A hierarchical, non-linear data structure of nodes connected by edges, with one root and no cycles.
The unique top node of a tree, which has no parent.
A node with no children.
A tree in which each node has at most two children, commonly called left and right.
A binary tree ordered so values in the left subtree are smaller and values in the right subtree are larger than the node value.

points: Every non-root node has one parent; a child may itself have children, and a node with none is a leaf.
A binary search tree supports search, insertion and deletion by comparing the target with each node and choosing left or right.
An in-order traversal (left, node, right) of a binary search tree visits values in ascending order.
Pre-order (node, left, right) and post-order (left, right, node) traversals are useful for copying/serialising and deleting a tree respectively.
Searching and insertion take O(log n) in a balanced search tree but can degrade to O(n) if the tree becomes a chain.

A linked implementation stores data and child references per node; an array representation can store children at indices 2i and 2i+1 (with a consistent indexing convention), but may waste space for sparse trees.
Deleting a search-tree node requires handling a leaf, a node with one child, or a node with two children (replace it with an in-order predecessor or successor).

title: Flipped - Data structures part 5 - Hash tables
hints: Candidates need to have an understanding of the behaviour of hash tables.
Candidates need to be able be aware of how hash tables can be implemented.

definitions.definition: A data structure that stores key-value records in an array, using a hash function to calculate an array index.
A value used to identify a record and supplied to the hash function.
A deterministic function that maps a key to an index within a table.
A situation where different keys produce the same table index.
The proportion of table slots that are occupied, commonly number of stored items divided by table capacity.

points: To insert or find a record, calculate the key’s hash index and inspect the corresponding slot; average lookup can be O(1).
A collision occurs even with a valid hash function when distinct keys map to the same finite set of slots.
Separate chaining stores colliding records in a list (or bucket) at the calculated slot; lookup must search that chain.
Open addressing searches for another free slot after a collision, for example by linear probing; lookup must repeat the same probe sequence.
Deletion in open addressing needs care (often a deleted marker) so searches do not incorrectly stop at a slot vacated by deletion.
A good hash function is fast and distributes likely keys evenly; clustering and a high load factor increase collisions and reduce performance.
When a table becomes too full it can be resized and entries rehashed; this uses extra time and memory during resizing.

title: Flipped - Data structures part 1 - Linked lists (operations)
hints: How to create, traverse, add data to and remove data from linked lists. (This can be either using arrays and procedural programming or an object-oriented approach).

Candidates should have experience of implementing linked lists in a variety of contexts, for example through a procedural program, through a different data structure and through an object-oriented approach.
Candidates need to be able to read, trace and write code to implement linked lists.

definitions.definition: The reference or index to the first linked-list node; it is null/sentinel when the list is empty.
A record containing a value and a next reference/index (plus a previous link in a doubly linked list).
Visiting nodes in sequence by following links from the head until the target or end is reached.
A linked chain of unused array positions available for allocation as list nodes.

points: To create an empty list, initialise its head to null (or a sentinel); for an array implementation also initialise a free-list or allocation index.
To traverse, start at head and repeatedly follow next until null, processing each node once; do not follow a stale or invalid link.
To insert at the head, set the new node’s next to the old head, then update head to the new node.
To insert after a known node, point the new node to the known node’s former successor, then point the known node to the new node.
To remove the head, set head to head.next; to remove a later node, make its predecessor point to the removed node’s successor and release the node.
Check empty-list, first-node, last-node and missing-value cases; update tail or previous links as required for the chosen implementation.
In a procedural array version, maintain data and next arrays plus head/free indices; in an object-oriented version, encapsulate value/next in Node and head/operations in a list class.
Trace code by recording head and each node’s value and link after every assignment; ensure removed nodes are not still reachable and reusable slots return to the free list.

title: Flipped - Data structures part 2 - Graphs (operations)
hints: How to create, traverse, add data to and remove data from graphs. (This can be either using arrays and procedural programming or an object-oriented approach).

Candidates should have experience of implementing graphs in a variety of contexts, for example through a procedural program, through a different data structure and through an object-oriented approach.
Candidates need to be able to read, trace and write code to implement graphs.

definitions.definition: A two-dimensional array in which entry [i][j] records the edge or weight from vertex i to vertex j.
A collection of lists, one per vertex, containing its neighbours and optionally edge weights.
A set or marker array recording vertices already processed during traversal.
A traversal that follows an unvisited neighbour as far as possible before backtracking.
A traversal that visits vertices in increasing number of edges from the start, typically using a queue.

points: Create vertices first and represent each edge in the selected structure; an undirected edge must be recorded in both directions, while a directed edge is recorded only from source to destination.
For a matrix, add/remove an edge by setting/clearing the appropriate cell (both symmetric cells if undirected); for weighted graphs store/remove the weight.
For an adjacency list, add an edge to the relevant neighbour list(s); removal requires finding and deleting the neighbour entry.
To traverse, initialise all vertices as unvisited, mark a start vertex when discovered, then process its unvisited neighbours so cycles do not cause infinite traversal.
DFS can be implemented recursively or with a stack; BFS uses a queue and is suitable for finding the fewest-edge path in an unweighted graph.
Removing a vertex requires removing its own neighbour data and all references to it; keep vertex identifiers/indexes consistent if the representation is compacted.
Procedural code can use arrays/lists and vertex indexes; an object-oriented version can define Vertex/Graph classes and methods for adding, removing and traversing.
Trace graph code by drawing the current edge set or adjacency table/list and the visited order; disconnected components require starting again at an unvisited vertex if all vertices must be visited.

title: Flipped - Data structures part 3 - Stacks & queues (operations)
hints: How to create, traverse, add data to and remove data from stacks & queues. (This can be either using arrays and procedural programming or an object-oriented approach).

Candidates should have experience of implementing stacks & queues in a variety of contexts, for example through a procedural program, through a different data structure and through an object-oriented approach.
Candidates need to be able to read, trace and write code to implement stacks & queues.

definitions.definition: Add an item to the top of a stack.
Remove and return the most recently pushed item from a stack.
Add an item at the rear of a queue.
Remove and return the item at the front of a queue.
A bounded array queue in which front and rear indexes wrap around to reuse slots.

points: For an array stack, push increments top then stores the item (or stores then increments, consistently); pop reads top then decrements it. Check full/empty before operating.
For a linked stack, push links a new node to the old top and updates top; pop updates top to top.next and returns/releases the old top.
For a simple queue, enqueue stores at rear and advances rear; dequeue reads front and advances front, with an explicit empty condition.
In a circular queue, advance an index with (index + 1) modulo capacity; use a count or reserved slot to distinguish full from empty.
A linked queue maintains front and rear references: enqueue links after rear and updates rear; dequeue advances front, setting rear null when the last node is removed.
A stack/queue has no arbitrary-position access in its abstract interface; traversal, if required, must preserve or restore the original order.
Procedural implementations use indexes and arrays; object-oriented implementations can hide storage and expose push/pop or enqueue/dequeue methods.
Test empty, one-item, full (bounded array), wrap-around, and repeated add/remove cases; trace the data and index/reference values after each operation.

title: Flipped - Data structures part 4 - Trees (operations)
hints: How to create, traverse, add data to and remove data from trees. (This can be either using arrays and procedural programming or an object-oriented approach).
Candidates should have experience of implementing trees in a variety of contexts, for example through a procedural program, through a different data structure and through an object-oriented approach.
Candidates need to be able to read, trace and write code to implement trees.

definitions.definition: A binary tree where left-subtree keys are smaller and right-subtree keys are larger than the node key.
Visit left subtree, node, then right subtree.
A parent is the node directly above another node; the lower node is its child.
A node together with all of its descendants.

points: Create a tree with a null root; insert the first value as root, then compare each later key and follow left/right links until a null child is found.
Search begins at root and repeatedly compares the target with the current key; equality is found, smaller follows left and larger follows right.
In-order traversal outputs BST values in sorted order; pre-order and post-order visit the node at different points and can be implemented recursively or with a stack.
Delete a leaf by disconnecting it from its parent; delete a node with one child by linking the parent directly to that child.
For a node with two children, replace its value with the in-order successor (smallest in right subtree) or predecessor, then delete that replacement node.
A linked implementation stores left/right references and optionally parent references; an array version uses child indexes, but unbalanced trees can leave many unused positions.
Object-oriented code can define a node class and tree methods; procedural code can pass root and node references/indexes explicitly.
Trace with a tree diagram and record comparisons/link changes; test empty tree, duplicate-key policy, leaf/root deletion, one-child and two-child deletion.

title: Flipped - Data structures part 5 - Hash tables (operations)
hints: How to create, traverse, add data to and remove data from hash tables. (This can be either using arrays and procedural programming or an object-oriented approach).

Candidates should have experience of implementing hash tables in a variety of contexts, for example through a procedural program, through a different data structure and through an object-oriented approach.
Candidates need to be able to read, trace and write code to implement hash tables.

definitions.definition: A function that converts a key to a valid table index.
Two different keys map to the same table index.
Collision resolution that checks successive table positions until a suitable slot is found.
Collision resolution that stores multiple records in a list or bucket associated with one index.

points: Create a table with a fixed capacity and empty-slot markers; choose a deterministic hash function that returns an index in range, for example key modulo table size for numeric keys.
Insert by hashing the key and storing the record in the selected slot; if occupied, resolve the collision using the defined method.
With linear probing, test the next positions (wrapping modulo capacity) until an empty slot is found; stop if every slot has been checked.
With chaining, add the record to the bucket/list at the hashed index; search checks each record in that chain for a matching key.
Search must apply the same hash and collision-resolution sequence as insertion; probing may stop at a genuinely never-used empty slot but not at a deleted marker.
Deletion can clear a chained record directly; in open addressing use a tombstone/deleted marker or reinsert following entries so later searches still work.
A high load factor increases collisions; handle a full table by reporting failure or resizing and rehashing all records.

A procedural implementation uses arrays and indexes; an object-oriented table can encapsulate the array, hash, and insert/search/delete methods. Trace the probe sequence or bucket contents for each key.

title: Flipped - Define problems using Boolean logic
hints: Candidates should be familiar with AND, OR, NOT and XOR.
Candidates should be familiar with the logic of each Boolean operator, and the truth tables.

definitions.definition: A logical value that is either true (1) or false (0).
A Boolean operator that returns true only when both operands are true.
A Boolean operator that returns true when at least one operand is true.
A unary Boolean operator that reverses its operand: true becomes false and false becomes true.
Exclusive OR; it returns true when exactly one of its two operands is true.

points: XOR truth table: 00→0, 01→1, 10→1, 11→0; equal inputs produce false.
NOT truth table: 0→1 and 1→0; NOT has one input, unlike the binary operators.
Boolean operators express conditions in a problem, for example access = hasPassword AND accountActive.
Use brackets to make precedence explicit; NOT applies to its operand, and truth tables can verify the result for every input combination.
For n independent Boolean inputs, a complete truth table has 2ⁿ input rows.

title: Flipped - Karnaugh maps
hints: Candidates should have an understanding that Boolean expressions can be simplified and should have experience of simplifying expressions using Karnaugh maps.
Candidates should be able to create, complete and interpret Karnaugh maps to simplify Boolean expressions.

definitions.definition: A grid representation of a truth table arranged so adjacent cells differ in only one input variable, used to simplify Boolean expressions.
A product term representing one truth-table input combination for which the output is 1.
K-map cells whose input combinations differ in exactly one variable; map edges also wrap around as adjacent.
A product term covering one or more output-1 cells without covering any output-0 cell.

points: For n variables, draw 2ⁿ cells and label rows/columns in Gray-code order (for example 00, 01, 11, 10), so neighbouring cells change one bit.
Transfer each truth-table output into its corresponding cell; place 1s for true outputs and 0s for false outputs.
Group adjacent 1s into rectangles containing 1, 2, 4, 8, … cells; groups may wrap across opposite edges and may overlap.
Choose large groups to eliminate as many variables as possible, while ensuring every 1 is covered at least once; use the fewest groups practicable.
For each group, retain only variables that stay constant throughout it; remove variables that change, then AND the retained literals to make the simplified term.
OR the terms from all groups to form the simplified sum-of-products expression; a variable fixed at 0 appears complemented and one fixed at 1 appears uncomplemented.
Check the result against the original truth table, including isolated 1s and edge-adjacent cells; use don’t-care cells only when supplied and only to simplify.

title: Flipped - Logic gates & truth tables
hints: Candidates should be able to construct logic gate diagrams from a Boolean expression and vice-versa.
Candidates should be able to construct truth tables from Boolean expressions and logic gate diagrams.

definitions.definition: An electronic circuit that performs a Boolean operation on one or more binary inputs to produce an output.
A table listing every input combination and the corresponding output(s) of a Boolean expression or circuit.
A NOT-AND gate; its output is false only when all inputs are true.
A NOT-OR gate; its output is true only when all inputs are false.
A graphical representation of logic gates connected to implement a Boolean function.

points: AND outputs 1 only for inputs 11; OR outputs 1 for 01, 10 and 11; NOT inverts its single input.
XOR outputs 1 when its two inputs differ; NAND is the inverse of AND and NOR is the inverse of OR.
Translate an expression into gates by applying each operator to its operands; parentheses or precedence determine which gate outputs feed later gates.
Translate a gate diagram into an expression by naming each intermediate output and combining inputs according to each gate.
For n input variables, list all 2ⁿ input combinations; evaluate each gate/intermediate expression row by row to construct the output column.
For a multi-output circuit, calculate a separate output column for each output, reusing intermediate results where appropriate.
Verify equivalence by checking that the expression, diagram and truth table produce the same output for every input combination.

title: Flipped - Simplifying Boolean algebra
hints: Candidates should be aware of the given De Morgan’s laws and should be able to apply these to a Boolean statement.
Candidates should have experience of manipulating and simplifying Boolean statements using these rules of distribution, commutation, association and double negation.

definitions.definition: NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B).
NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B).
The order of operands can be changed: A AND B = B AND A, and A OR B = B OR A.
Grouping can be changed without changing the result: (A AND B) AND C = A AND (B AND C), similarly for OR.
NOT (NOT A) = A.

points: Distribution: A AND (B OR C) = (A AND B) OR (A AND C); A OR (B AND C) = (A OR B) AND (A OR C).
Use commutation to reorder terms and association to regroup them so matching terms can be combined.
Apply De Morgan’s laws by complementing each operand and changing AND to OR, or OR to AND, when negation covers a bracket.
Double negation removes two NOT operators; take care not to remove a single negation or alter its scope.
Useful identities include A OR 0 = A, A AND 1 = A, A OR 1 = 1, and A AND 0 = 0.
Idempotent and complement identities include A OR A = A, A AND A = A, A OR NOT A = 1, and A AND NOT A = 0.
Simplify one law at a time and preserve equivalent meaning; confirm with a truth table if unsure.

title: Flipped - Half & full adders
hints: Candidates need to understand the purpose and function of an adder circuit, and the difference between a half and full adder.
They should be able to recognise and draw the logic gates and truth tables for full and half adders.

definitions.definition: A combinational circuit that adds two one-bit inputs and produces a sum and carry, but has no carry-in input.
A combinational circuit that adds two one-bit inputs and a carry-in, producing a sum and carry-out.
The least significant output bit of binary addition.
An output bit passed to the next more significant position when a binary column’s total exceeds 1.

points: A half adder has inputs A,B and outputs Sum = A XOR B and Carry = A AND B.
Half-adder truth table (A B : Sum Carry): 00:00, 01:10, 10:10, 11:01.
A full adder adds A, B and carry-in Cin; Sum = A XOR B XOR Cin.
Full-adder carry-out Cout = (A AND B) OR (A AND Cin) OR (B AND Cin); it is 1 when at least two inputs are 1.
A full adder can be built from two half adders and an OR gate combining their carry outputs.
Connecting full adders in series lets each stage pass its carry-out to the next bit position, enabling multi-bit addition; carry propagation can limit speed.

title: Flipped - D-type flip flops
hints: Candidates need to understand the purpose and principles of D type flip flops and how and where they are used in a computer.
They should be able to recognise how they can be triggered by a clock pulse (see practice paper 2 for an example).
Candidates are not expected to memorise the logic gates that make up a D-type flip flop.

definitions.definition: A bistable circuit that stores one bit and, when triggered, copies its D input to its Q output.
A regular timing signal whose active edge or level controls when a sequential circuit updates.
A circuit behaviour in which state changes at a specified transition of the clock, rather than continuously.
A circuit with two stable states, representing binary 0 and 1.

points: A D-type flip-flop stores one bit; its output Q retains the stored value between triggering clock events.
At the active clock edge, the value at D is copied to Q; changes to D between active edges do not immediately alter Q.
The flip-flop is a sequential circuit because its output depends on stored previous state as well as current input/timing.
Flip-flops can form registers by combining multiple one-bit storage elements, one per bit.
They are used to store data and state in registers, counters, synchronisers and other clocked processor/digital circuits.
A clock provides coordinated timing so components update in step; edge-triggering avoids uncontrolled changes during a clock cycle.
A D-type flip-flop should not be confused with combinational logic, whose outputs respond directly to current inputs and have no stored state.

title: Flipped - Data Protection Act
hints: Candidates need to have an understanding of the need for and purpose of laws relating to the use of computers.

Candidates should be familiar with the purpose and role of the Data Protection Act, candidates will need to understand the different rules that are within the DPA and how these impact the use of computers and the storage of data by organisations, this should include what organisations can and cannot do.

We are aware the law is constantly changing and some of the mentioned laws (most notably the DPA) are likely to change over the course of the specification. Answers will be accepted that use an interpretation of the law based on when the specification was started or when the examination was sat.

definitions.definition: Information relating to an identified or identifiable living individual.
The individual whom personal data is about.
The person or organisation that determines why and how personal data is processed.
A person or organisation that processes personal data on behalf of a controller.
A legal requirement governing fair, lawful and responsible handling of personal data.

points: UK data protection law is now the UK GDPR together with the Data Protection Act 2018; older exam materials may refer to the 1998 Act, so apply the law relevant to the question/context.
Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently, for specified purposes, and collected only when adequate, relevant and necessary.
Data must be accurate and kept up to date; inaccurate data should be corrected or erased.
Personal data should not be kept longer than necessary and must be protected against unauthorised or unlawful processing, loss, destruction or damage.
