Organisations must be able to demonstrate compliance and must use appropriate technical and organisational security measures; they must not use data incompatibly with its stated purpose.
Individuals have rights including access to their personal data, rectification and, in applicable circumstances, erasure, restriction, objection and data portability.
Organisations should establish a lawful basis, provide privacy information, control access, set retention periods and respond properly to subject requests and reportable breaches.
The law protects individuals while allowing legitimate processing; serious non-compliance can lead to regulatory enforcement and significant fines.

title: Flipped - Computer Misuse Act
hints: Candidates need to understand the purpose and principles of the Computer Misuse Act, including the actions that it prohibits.

definitions.definition: Accessing computer material without permission or exceeding permission granted.
Intentionally changing computer data or impairing a system without authority.
UK legislation criminalising specified unauthorised access to and interference with computer systems and data.
Software designed to perform unauthorised or harmful actions, such as stealing data or disrupting systems.

points: The Act makes it an offence to cause a computer to perform a function with intent to obtain unauthorised access to programs or data (hacking).
It separately criminalises unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate further offences, such as fraud or theft.
Unauthorised acts intended to impair a computer’s operation or the reliability of data are offences; this can include deploying malware or denial-of-service activity.
Making, supplying or obtaining articles (including software or credentials) for use in relevant computer offences can also be an offence.
Permission is central: testing or accessing a system without authorisation can be illegal even if no data is ultimately stolen or changed.
The Act protects confidentiality, integrity and availability of computer systems and data; organisations can reduce risk with access controls, monitoring and authorised security testing.
It applies to individuals and organisations; offences can result in criminal penalties, including imprisonment and/or fines.

title: Flipped - Copyright Design & Patents Act
hints: Candidates need to understand the purpose and principles of the Copyright and Patents Act, including the actions that it prohibits.

definitions.definition: An intellectual property right that protects original works, including software, from specified unauthorised copying and use.
The person or organisation holding the exclusive rights to a protected work.
Terms granting permission to use software while setting limits on actions such as copying or redistribution.
Creations of the mind, such as software, music, writing and inventions, protected by legal rights.

points: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects original works including computer programs, text, music, films and images.
Copyright generally arises automatically; the owner controls acts such as copying, issuing copies, adapting and communicating the work to the public.
Installing or copying software beyond the permission in its licence, or distributing unauthorised copies, can infringe copyright.
A purchaser normally receives a licence to use software, not ownership of the copyright; licence terms may restrict number of installations, copying or modification.
Exceptions such as limited permitted acts may apply in defined circumstances; they do not give a general right to pirate or share commercial software.
Infringement can harm creators and organisations through lost revenue and can lead to civil remedies and, for certain deliberate commercial infringements, criminal penalties.
Organisations should use properly licensed software, keep licence records and train staff; users should check permissions before copying, adapting or sharing content.

title: Flipped - Investigatory Powers Act
hints: Candidates need to understand the purpose and principles of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act, and what this allows in the interception and monitoring of electronic communication.
Candidates need to understand how the regulations impact organisations and the use of computers and electronic communication.

definitions.definition: Acquiring the contents of a communication while it is being transmitted.
Information about a communication, such as who communicated, when, where or how, rather than its content.
UK legislation setting legal powers and safeguards for interception, communications data acquisition and related investigatory techniques.
The Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000, an earlier UK law governing certain surveillance and interception powers, substantially updated by later legislation.

points: The Investigatory Powers Act 2016 provides powers for specified public authorities to obtain communications data and, under legal authorisation, intercept communications for defined purposes.
Interception concerns message content; communications data concerns metadata such as sender, recipient, time and service used.
Powers are subject to statutory tests, authorisation procedures and oversight; they are not a general permission for any organisation to read any communication.
The Act includes provisions concerning lawful interception, warrants, retention/access to data and oversight by independent bodies, including the Investigatory Powers Commissioner.
RIPA 2000 historically regulated interception and surveillance; current answers should distinguish it from the later Investigatory Powers Act where relevant.
Organisations may have duties to comply with valid lawful notices, while also needing to protect customers’ confidentiality and personal data and restrict access to authorised staff.
Monitoring or interception without proper authority can breach privacy, data-protection law and other legal duties; organisations should have clear policies and legal review.

section: SLR 17 – Ethical moral and cultural issues
title: Flipped – Computers in the workplace & Computers for automated decision making
hints: The individual (moral), social (ethical) and cultural opportunities and risks of digital technology:
Computers in the workforce
Automated decision making
Candidates need to understand what is meant by moral, social, ethical and cultural issues in relation to the use of computers.

Candidates need to understand how the use of computers, and the increasing use of computers in the work force has moral, social, ethical and cultural implications and risks to a variety of people such as the employees, employers, society and organisations.

Candidates need to understand how the use of computers to make decisions automatically has moral, social, ethical and cultural implications and risks to a variety of people such as those people who make the decisions, the people the decisions affect, and the need for additional collection of information to ensure the decisions are accurate and valid.

definitions.definition: A question about what an individual considers right or wrong.
An effect of technology on relationships, communities or society as a whole.
A question about fair and responsible conduct, often involving competing rights or interests.
An effect of technology shaped by the beliefs, customs, language or practices of a group.
Using a computer system or algorithm to make or recommend a decision with limited or no human involvement.

points: Workplace automation can increase productivity, consistency and safety by handling repetitive or hazardous tasks.
Automation may displace workers, reduce job security or deskill roles; employers may gain efficiency while employees and communities bear transition costs.
Technology can create new jobs and enable flexible or remote work, but benefits may be uneven and a digital skills gap can widen inequality.
Automated decisions can process large datasets quickly and consistently, but biased or inaccurate training data can produce discriminatory outcomes.
Affected people may not understand or be able to challenge an opaque decision; human review, explanation, testing and appeal mechanisms improve accountability.
Collecting more information may improve prediction but increases privacy, security and consent risks; only necessary, relevant data should be used.
Responsibility should be clear between developers, employers and organisations using a system; assess impacts on employees, customers, society and cultural groups.

section: SLR 17 – Ethical moral and cultural issues
title: Flipped - Artificial Intelligence & Environmental effects
hints: The individual (moral), social (ethical) and cultural opportunities and risks of digital technology:
Artificial intelligence
Environmental effects
Candidates need to understand how the development of artificial intelligence has moral, social, ethical and cultural impacts on a variety of people.
Candidates need to understand how the environmental effects of computers (such as disposal, energy use) have moral, social, ethical and cultural implications.

definitions.definition: Computer systems performing tasks associated with human intelligence, such as learning, prediction or language understanding.
A method in which a system learns patterns from data to make predictions or decisions rather than following only explicitly programmed rules.
Discarded electrical and electronic equipment and its components.
The greenhouse-gas emissions associated with an activity, product or organisation.

points: AI can improve diagnosis, accessibility, translation, forecasting and automation, but errors can cause harm when outputs are relied on without human judgement.
Training data may encode existing bias; AI decisions can reproduce or amplify discrimination and may be difficult to explain.
AI can displace some work while creating other roles; people may need retraining, and impacts can fall unevenly across communities.
AI systems require data and computing resources; privacy, surveillance, consent and accountability are concerns when personal data is used.
Computers consume electricity during manufacture, use and data-centre operation, contributing to emissions if energy comes from fossil fuels.
Electronic devices contain valuable and hazardous materials; frequent replacement and unsafe disposal waste resources and can harm health and the environment.
Longer device lifetimes, repair, reuse, recycling, energy-efficient hardware and renewable electricity can reduce environmental impact, though recycling itself also uses energy.

section: SLR 17 – Ethical moral and cultural issues
title: Flipped – Censorship & Monitor Behaviour
hints: The individual (moral), social (ethical) and cultural opportunities and risks of digital technology:
Censorship and the Internet
Monitor behaviour
Candidates need to understand how the Internet and censorship on the Internet has moral, social, ethical and cultural implications.
Candidates need to understand the moral, social, ethical and cultural implications of using computers to monitor behaviour (such as CCTV, tracking phone calls, GPS, monitoring emails).

definitions.definition: The control or suppression of access to or publication of information or expression.
Systematic observation or collection of information about people or their activities.
Closed-circuit television used to capture and transmit video to a limited set of monitors or recorders.
Using satellite-based positioning data to determine and record a device’s location.

points: Internet censorship can limit harmful, illegal or age-inappropriate content and protect people, but excessive blocking can restrict freedom of expression and access to information.
Filtering may be imposed by governments, schools, employers or platforms; errors can block legitimate material or fail to block harmful content.
CCTV, email/call logs, web monitoring and GPS tracking can support safety, security and investigations, but can intrude on privacy and chill lawful behaviour.
Continuous monitoring can affect trust and workplace morale; people may change behaviour because they know they are being observed.
Location and communication records can reveal sensitive routines or relationships; collected data must be secured and retained only as necessary.
Monitoring should have a clear lawful purpose, be proportionate and transparent, and use the least intrusive effective method.
There is a balance between public safety and individual rights; oversight, access controls, retention limits and routes to challenge misuse reduce risks.

section: SLR 17 – Ethical moral and cultural issues
title: Flipped – Analyse personal information
hints: The individual (moral), social (ethical) and cultural opportunities and risks of digital technology:
Analyse personal information
Candidates need to understand the moral, social, ethical and cultural implications of using computers to analyse personal information (such as the gathering, storing and analysing of medical records)

definitions.definition: Information that identifies or relates to an individual, including sensitive details such as health data.
The computational examination of data to identify patterns, trends or relationships and derive conclusions.
Automated processing of personal data to evaluate or predict aspects of an individual, such as health, behaviour or preferences.
Processing data so that individuals are not identifiable by means reasonably likely to be used.

points: Analysing records such as medical data can reveal trends, support diagnosis and treatment planning, and improve public-health decisions.
Combining datasets may expose identities or sensitive facts even when data was thought anonymous; robust de-identification and access controls are important.
Incorrect, incomplete or unrepresentative data can produce misleading conclusions and unfair treatment, especially for under-represented groups.
Use of personal information should be lawful, transparent, purpose-limited and based on an appropriate legal basis; collect only data needed for the task.
Health data is especially sensitive: unauthorised access or disclosure can cause stigma, distress, discrimination or financial harm.
Individuals should be informed about uses where required and have applicable data-protection rights; organisations need security, retention and breach procedures.
Balance societal benefits of research and service improvement against privacy, consent, confidentiality and the risk of re-identification.

section: SLR 17 – Ethical moral and cultural issues
title: Flipped - Moral, social & ethical issues
hints: The individual (moral), social (ethical) and cultural opportunities and risks of digital technology:
Piracy and offensive communications
Layout, colour paradigms and character sets.

Candidates need to understand how piracy and offensive communications have moral, social, ethical and cultural implications and risks to a variety of people such as content creators, organisations, Internet users and wider society.

Candidates should understand issues such as the illegal copying and distribution of software, music, films and other digital content, and how this can affect individuals and organisations financially.

Candidates should also understand how computers and the Internet can be used to send offensive, abusive, threatening or misleading communications, and the impacts these may have on individuals, groups and society.

Candidates need to consider the balance between freedom of expression, preventing harm, protecting intellectual property, and the responsibilities of users and organisations when using computer systems and online services.

Candidates need to understand how different cultures impact on the use of and creation of computers and programs. For example languages make use of different characters, and how this in turn impacts the use of character sets. Some languages read left to right, and others right to left.

Candidates should understand how colours have different meanings in different cultures for example red means danger in one culture, and luck in another. Candidates need to consider how these will impact the creation of computer applications.

definitions.definition: Unauthorised copying, sharing, downloading or distribution of copyrighted digital content.
A communication that is abusive, threatening, harassing or otherwise unlawful or harmful.
A defined collection of characters and the numeric codes used to represent them digitally.
A widely used character-encoding standard assigning code points to characters across many writing systems.
A set of language- and region-specific conventions, including text direction, formats and cultural presentation.

points: Piracy of software, music, films and other content deprives creators and organisations of income, can undermine jobs and may breach copyright law or licence terms.
Unauthorised downloads and copies can expose users to malware, poor-quality files and legal consequences; legitimate services and licences provide lawful access.
Online anonymity and rapid distribution can enable abusive, threatening or misleading messages, causing distress, reputational damage and wider social harm.
Responses to offensive communications should protect people from harm while respecting lawful expression; platforms and users have responsibilities to report, moderate and communicate safely.
Applications must use character encodings capable of representing users’ languages; Unicode supports characters from many scripts, unlike limited legacy character sets.
Text direction varies: many scripts are left-to-right, while Arabic and Hebrew are generally right-to-left; interfaces must support bidirectional text and correct ordering.
Colours and symbols have culture-specific meanings (for example, red can signal danger in some contexts and luck or celebration in others); designers should test with intended users.
Localisation should account for language, character coverage, text expansion, layout, date/number conventions, colour meaning and accessibility rather than merely translating words.
